cards.name: Takamimusubi
cards.flavor: The first-born deity in the Kojiki, 'the High Deity who gives birth to the origin of things,' invoked at the opening of the creation sequence.
cards.long: Takamimusubi (高皇産霊神; also read Kamimusubi, 'the high divine origin') is the first divine being named in the Kojiki's opening passage: 'In the time when the heavenly high plain had just come into being, first of all was born the high divine origin of heavenly things, Kamimusubi' [S1]. He is generally treated as a primordial deity associated with the origin of things rather than a figure with a developed myth of his own. His exact nature—whether a personified principle of origin, a progenitor, or a ritual formula—is debated; the Kojiki's account is terse and heavily ritualized [S1][S2]. He is sometimes paired with two younger brothers (Takamimusubi's 'younger brothers'), but the genealogy of these primordial figures is one of the least stable in the corpus.
cards.image_credit: Takamimusubi · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Amenominakanushi
cards.flavor: The primordial deity of the High Plain of Heaven (Takamagahara), who in the Kojiki 'gave birth to' or commanded the birth of the creator pair Izanagi and Izanami.
cards.long: Amenominakanushi ('Lord of the Center of the High Plain of Heaven') is the deity of the heavenly highland in the Kojiki. In the creation passage, after the primordial beings are named, it is the 'high plain of heaven' and its deities that produce the pair who will form the islands: the Kojiki says the kami of the high plain 'gave birth' to Izanagi and Izanami and ordered them to shape and settle the earthly islands [S1]. The Nihon Shoki gives a parallel but differently-worded account, and the precise mechanism (whether 'birth' is literal or a ritual/creative command) is one of the classic ambiguities in Japanese cosmogony [S1][S2]. He functions less as a character and more as the heavenly authority from which the creative pair is sent.

cards.name: Izanagi
cards.flavor: Male member of the divine creator pair who, with his sister-wife Izanami, stirred the brine of the sea to form the Japanese islands and gave birth to the high deities.
cards.long: Izanagi ('He who Invites') is the male progenitor in the Kojiki's creation. He and Izanami stand on the Floating Bridge of Heaven (Ame-no-ukihashi) and, using the jeweled spear Ame-no-nuhokohe, stir the brine below; the salt that drips forms the first island, Onogoro [S1]. There they wed and, over a series of 'birthings,' produce the great islands of Japan and then the deities (kami) who attend them [S1]. After Izanami's death in giving birth to the fire god, Izanagi follows her to the Land of Yomi, discovers her decayed body, and flees; the ensuing separation of the clean (heavenly) and polluted (underworld) realms, and Izanagi's subsequent purification (misogi), generate many further kami [S1]. He is thus a creator, a threshold-crosser between the living and dead realms, and a figure of ritual purification [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: The God Izanagi and Goddess Izanami · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain (Met Open Access)

cards.name: Izanami
cards.flavor: Female member of the divine creator pair who, with Izanagi, formed the Japanese islands; after dying in childbirth, became associated with the Land of Yomi (the dead).
cards.long: Izanami ('He/She who Invites') is the female progenitor who, together with Izanagi, forms the islands and gives birth to the deities [S1]. In the Kojiki, she dies in giving birth to the fire god Kagutsuchi, her body consumed by the fire of childbirth [S1]. Grief-stricken, Izanagi descends to Yomi to bring her back; finding her decayed and attended by 'the eight devils of rotting,' he flees, and the two are separated at the threshold—the origin of the divide between the clean world of the living and the polluted realm of the dead [S1]. Thereafter Izanami is associated with Yomi and with death, while Izanagi remains with the living and heavenly realms [S1][S2]. She thus spans creation and mortality, a pivotal figure in Japanese eschatology.
cards.image_credit: Izanagi and Izanami Creating the First Japanese Islands · Massachusetts Fine Arts (via Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain

cards.name: Amaterasu
cards.flavor: The Sun Goddess and supreme deity of the Shinto high pantheon; ancestress of the Japanese imperial line and the central figure of the Heavenly Rock-Cave myth.
cards.long: Amaterasu-ōmikami ('Great Divine Illuminator of Heaven') is the sun goddess and, in later Shinto, the highest deity of the pantheon and the mythic ancestress of the imperial house [S1]. In the Kojiki she is born from Izanagi's left hand (with the jewel) during the birth-sequence after the islands are formed, and she is sent to rule over the High Plain of Heaven [S1]. Her brother Susanoo's violent misconduct leads to his banishment from heaven; when he departs, Amaterasu, in grief and fear, withdraws into the Heavenly Rock-Cave (Ame-no-Ohafutsu), plunging the world into darkness. The other kami, led by the dancing goddess Ame-no-Uzume, lure her back out, restoring light [S1]. From her line descends the heavenly prince Ninigi and, ultimately, the Japanese emperors [S1][S2]. She is the patron of the Ise Grand Shrine and the symbolic center of state Shinto; the mirror Yata no Kagami, one of the three Imperial Regalia, is her emblem [S1].
cards.image_credit: Luring the Sun Goddess Amaterasu Out of a Cave with Music; Death of the Fire God · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain (Met Open Access)

cards.name: Tsukuyomi
cards.flavor: The Moon God, born of the creator pair; in the Kojiki he is estranged from Amaterasu after desecrating the weaving hall, marking the separation of sun and moon.
cards.long: Tsukuyomi-no-Mikoto ('He who Illuminates the Night') is the moon god, born in the Kojiki's sequence (from Izanagi's right hand) alongside his siblings Amaterasu and Susanoo [S1]. In the Kojiki, he visits the Palace of the Weaving of Garments (where the goddess Ukehimuka weaves) and kills her there; because the act pollutes the sacred weaving place, Amaterasu is disgusted and declares that she and Tsukuyomi shall no longer share the same palace—the mythic basis for the separate courses of sun and moon [S1]. He is thus a figure of the night and of the separation of the solar and lunar realms. His role is relatively minor in the corpus; he has little developed mythology beyond this estrangement [S1][S2].

cards.name: Susanoo
cards.flavor: The storm and sea god, younger brother of Amaterasu; famed for slaying the eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi and for his role in the subjugation of the island (Kuniyurinshi).
cards.long: Susanoo-no-Mikoto ('Fierce Male of the Waves') is the storm/sea god, the last and most violent of the three high deities born of the creator pair [S1]. In the Kojiki his disruptive misconduct (desecrating the heavenly rice fields and weaving hall) leads to his banishment from Takamagahara to the earthly realm [S1]. On his way down to Izumo he meets the weeping parents of a family whose daughters are being devoured by the eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi; Susanoo slays the beast, and in its tail finds the sword Kusanagi (Ame-murakumo-no-tsurugi) [S1]. He rescues and marries the last daughter, Kushinada-hime [S1]. Later he takes part in the subjugation of the island deity Ōkuninushi (the Kuniyurinshi), working with the thunder god Takemikazuchi [S1]. He is thus a liminal, violent, and heroic figure—storm, sea, and monster-slayer—whose transgressions and triumphs both define him [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Susanoo-no-Mikoto Slays Yamata-no-Orochi in Izumo · Wikimedia Commons · Public domain
