cards.name: Kagutsuchi
cards.flavor: The Fire God, whose birth in the flames of childbirth kills his mother Izanami, driving the Kojiki's Yomi-separation episode.
cards.long: Kagutsuchi (also Hinode-no-Kami, 'Fire God') is the deity of fire, born in the Kojiki's sequence as the child whose birth kills his mother: Izanami, giving birth to him, is burned by the fire of childbirth and dies [S1]. His birth is the catalytic event of the myth: it sends Izanagi down to Yomi and produces the separation of the living and dead realms [S1]. He is associated with fire, heat, and (in some accounts) volcanic/mountain activity. He has little independent mythology beyond this pivotal, tragic birth [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Kagutsuchi · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Konohanasakuya-hime
cards.flavor: The 'Flower-Blossom' goddess of the earthly realm, daughter of Ōkuninushi, who marries the descending heavenly prince Ninigi and bears the imperial ancestor Hooroni.
cards.long: Konohanasakuya-hime ('Blossoming of the Wood-Flower') is the goddess of flowers and the earthly realm, a daughter of the island god Ōkuninushi [S1]. When the heavenly prince Ninigi descends to the middle land (Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni), she is the first earthly bride he takes; from their union is born (in the genealogy) the line that leads to the imperial ancestor Hooroni [S1]. She embodies the fertile, blossoming earth that the heavenly line is sent to rule. Her name is a poetic compound evoking the flowering of a tree (wood + flower + blossom). [S1][S2]
cards.image_credit: Konohanasakuya-hime · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Ninigi
cards.flavor: The 'Heavenly Prince' (grandson of Amaterasu) sent down to rule the middle land; central to the Tenson Kōryō (descent of the heavenly deity) and the founding of the imperial line.
cards.long: Ninigi-no-Mikoto is the heavenly prince, grandson of Amaterasu, sent down from Takamagahara to take rule of the middle land (Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni) [S1]. His descent (Tenson Kōryō) alights at Takachiho in Hyuga (Kyūshū) [S1]. On the way, guided by the crossroads god Sarutahiko, he is confronted by the island god Ōkuninushi and his retinue, who resist the heavenly takeover; after the contest (the throwing of the sword) and the subjugation (Kuniyurinshi), Ōkuninushi hands over the land and the sacred regalia [S1]. Ninigi takes the earthly bride Konohanasakuya-hime and later the heavenly bride Toyotama-hime (Amaterasu's daughter); their son Hooroni (Ōyahata) is the ancestor of the emperors [S1][S2]. He is thus the hinge figure between the heavenly and earthly realms and the founding link in the imperial genealogy.
cards.image_credit: Ninigi · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Toyotama-hime
cards.flavor: Daughter of Amaterasu and the 'heavenly bride' of Ninigi; when she gives birth to Hooroni at sea, she becomes the sea goddess (Watatsumi), the mythic origin of the sea.
cards.long: Toyotama-hime ('Abundant Jewel Princess'), also called Hohodemi, is a daughter of Amaterasu sent down as the 'heavenly bride' of the descending prince Ninigi [S1]. In the Kojiki she gives birth to their son Hooroni (Ōyahata) in a small hut (hori-hutsu) at sea; when Ninigi, impatient, opens the hut, smoke and blood issue and the sea is born—thereafter Toyotama-hime is identified with the sea as the goddess Watatsumi [S1]. She thus embodies the heavenly line's union with the earthly/sea realm and the mythic origin of the sea. The genealogy from her to the emperors (through Hooroni) is a key part of the imperial founding myth [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Toyotama-hime · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Hooroni (Ōyahata)
cards.flavor: Son of Ninigi and Toyotama-hime, born at sea; the direct ancestor in the mythic line leading to the Japanese emperors.
cards.long: Hooroni (Ōyahata-no-Mikoto) is the son of the heavenly prince Ninigi and his heavenly bride Toyotama-hime, born in the 'birth at sea' episode [S1]. He is the link in the mythic genealogy from the heavenly line to the historical (semi-legendary) emperors; the line proceeds Hooroni → Hibi → … → Emperor Jimmu (the first historical-legendary emperor) [S1][S2]. He is a genealogical figure rather than a character with developed mythology.
cards.image_credit: Hoori (Ōyahata) meeting the sea-king's daughter · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Ōkuninushi
cards.flavor: The 'Great Lord of the Country,' the powerful indigenous deity of the middle land who resists, then yields, the heavenly takeover (the Kuniyurinshi).
cards.long: Ōkuninushi-no-Kami ('Great Lord of the Country') is the powerful indigenous deity of the earthly realm (Ashihara-no-Nakatsukuni), especially associated with Izumo [S1]. In the Kojiki's Kuniyurinshi ('pacification/subjugation of the country') episode, when the heavenly prince Ninigi is sent down to rule, Ōkuninushi and his retinue (led by the crossroads god Sarutahiko) resist the heavenly takeover [S1]. After a contest—centered on the throwing of the sword and the subduing of Sarutahiko—Ōkuninushi is defeated and yields the land, handing over the three sacred regalia (mirror, jewel, sword) as pledge [S1]. Thereafter he is a deity of the earth, healing, and agriculture (especially in Izumo), but no longer the sovereign of the whole land. He is a complex figure: the displaced indigenous power who becomes a local, beneficent deity [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Ōkuninushi no Mikoto statue · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Kotohikone
cards.flavor: The 'Ever-Standing in the Country' deity, a mediator/alliance figure in the Kuniyurinshi who brokers the marriage tying the heavenly and earthly lines.
cards.long: Kotohikone-no-Mikoto ('Ever-Standing in the Country') is a deity of the earthly realm who, in the Kuniyurinshi episode, serves as a mediator and alliance figure [S1]. He is associated with the marriage/alliance that ties the heavenly line (Ninigi) to the earthly line, and with the yielding of the land by Ōkuninushi [S1]. His exact role—whether a separate deity, a title, or an aspect—varies; in some accounts he is the one who brokers the union and the handover of the regalia [S1][S2]. He is a minor but structurally important figure in the founding myth.

cards.name: Sarutahiko
cards.flavor: The 'Monkey-Field' crossroads god who guides the descending prince Ninigi through the earthly realm, and is subdued in the Kuniyurinshi contest.
cards.long: Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami ('Monkey-Field God') is a deity of crossroads and guidance, especially in Izumo [S1]. In the Kuniyurinshi he is the lead of Ōkuninushi's retinue who resists the heavenly prince Ninigi; he is the one who, carrying the sword, is subdued in the contest, clearing the way for the heavenly takeover [S1]. He is also the guide who leads Ninigi through the earthly realm on his descent [S1]. He is a liminal figure of the crossroads and the threshold between the heavenly and earthly realms [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Sarutahiko · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Ame-no-Uzume
cards.flavor: The 'Heavenly Dancing Goddess' whose dance, in the Rock-Cave myth, lures Amaterasu back out and restores the light.
cards.long: Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto ('Heavenly Uzume') is the dancing goddess who, in the Heavenly Rock-Cave myth, performs the central act of restoration [S1]. When Amaterasu withdraws into the cave and the world is dark, the other kami devise a plan; Ame-no-Uzume dances (a ritual kagura) on an upturned tub, and her dance, with the assembled kami's clamor, provokes Amaterasu's curiosity and joy, drawing her to the cave mouth so that she is lured back into the light [S1]. She is the embodiment of the dance that 'lures the sun back,' and the kagura (Shinto ritual dance) is ritually linked to her act [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Ame-no-Uzume · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Takemikazuchi
cards.flavor: The thunder/war god who throws the sword in the Kuniyurinshi contest and plays a role in luring Amaterasu from the cave.
cards.long: Takemikazuchi-no-Mikoto ('Sword Thunder God') is a deity of thunder and war [S1]. In the Kuniyurinshi episode he is the one who throws the sword (Kusanagi) from the high land to the middle land, hitting the target and demonstrating the heavenly gods' strength in the contest with Ōkuninushi's side [S1]. He also plays a role in the Rock-Cave myth, where the assembled deities (including him) make the clamor that draws Amaterasu out [S1]. He is a martial, thunder-associated figure in the high and earthly realms [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Takemikazuchi · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Kushinada-hime
cards.flavor: The last daughter of the family whose daughters were devoured by Yamata-no-Orochi; rescued and married by Susanoo after he slays the serpent.
cards.long: Kushinada-hime ('Comb-Field Princess') is the last of the eight daughters of the family in Izumo whose older sisters had been devoured by the eight-headed serpent Yamata-no-Orochi [S1]. Susanoo, on his way down to the earthly realm, learns of her impending fate, turns himself into a hair-comb, and has her wear it; when the serpent comes for her, he slays it and rescues her, and they marry [S1]. She is thus the 'rescued bride' of the Orochi myth, a figure of deliverance from the monster [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Susanoo rescues Kushinada-hime · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

sources.text: Toyohara Chikanobu: Susanoo rescues Kushinada Hime

cards.name: Yamata-no-Orochi
cards.flavor: The eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent that devours the daughters of the Izumo family and is slain by Susanoo, whose tail yields the sword Kusanagi.
cards.long: Yamata-no-Orochi ('Eight-Branched Great Serpent') is the great serpent monster of the Izumo region, with eight heads and eight tails [S1]. It devours the daughters of a local family one by one (seven of the eight), and the last, Kushinada-hime, is next [S1]. Susanoo slays the beast—traditionally by luring it with sweetened sake in eight vats and cutting it down—and in its tail he finds the sword Kusanagi (Ame-murakumo-no-tsurugi) [S1]. It is the archetypal Japanese serpent monster, a force of destructive chaos overcome by the hero-god [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Susanoo slays Yamata-no-Orochi in Izumo · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Inari
cards.flavor: The 'Rice' deity (Inari Ōkami) of rice, prosperity, and foxes, with the great Fushimi Inari shrine; a later (Heian-onward) development, not a Kojiki figure.
cards.long: Inari Ōkami is the deity of rice, prosperity, and the fox (kitsune), centered on the great Fushimi Inari Taisha in Kyōto [S1]. Unlike the high deities of the Kojiki, Inari is a later (Heian-period and later) development of Shinto, illustrating that the Japanese tradition continued to grow long after the 8th-century mythographic compilations [S1][S21]. The deity is often represented as a female figure and is attended by foxes, which serve as messengers. Inari's rise reflects the agricultural and mercantile concerns of later Japanese religion, and it shows that 'Japanese mythology' is not a closed 8th-century corpus but a living, accreting tradition [S1][S21].
cards.image_credit: Inari shrine painting by Kawanabe Kyosai · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

sources.text: Shinto: A Very Short Introduction (Sue Keown)

cards.name: Yamato Takeru
cards.flavor: A semi-legendary imperial prince-hero of the 7th-century tradition, famed for his campaigns; a literary/legendary hero rather than a Kojiki deity.
cards.long: Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto ('Brave Hero of Yamato') is a semi-legendary prince-hero of the Japanese imperial line, a central figure of later (7th-century and later) legend and the 'heroic' stratum of Japanese narrative [S2]. He is famed for his campaigns (the eastern and southern subjugations) and his death by a trick (the 'arrow that sings'). He belongs to the heroic/legendary layer rather than the primordial Kojiki theogony, and he illustrates the range of the Japanese tradition from cosmic theogony to imperial hero-legend [S1][S2][S21].

sources.text: Shinto: A Very Short Introduction (Sue Keown)

cards.name: Chaos
cards.flavor: The first 'gap' or 'yawn' of existence in Hesiod's Theogony — the void from which all else, including Night and Eros, first emerged.
cards.long: In Hesiod's Theogony, the very first thing is Chaos — a yawning gap, not a god in the anthropomorphic sense but the primordial void from which the earliest beings spring [S1]. From Chaos come Gaia (Earth), Tartarus (the deep abyss), Eros (attraction/love), and Nyx (Night) [S1]. Chaos is best understood as a cosmogonic principle — the empty space that makes differentiation possible — rather than a character. Later Orphic tradition recasts the origin differently (a cosmic egg, Phanes), a genuine variant we present alongside the Hesiodic account [S1][S5].

cards.name: Gaia
cards.flavor: Earth herself — the first solid being in Hesiod, mother of the Titans and mother of nearly every primordial lineage.
cards.long: Gaia (Earth) is, in Hesiod's Theogony, the second named being after Chaos: from Chaos came Gaia, the broad breast that is the foundation of all [S1]. She is a mother to an extraordinary degree — she gives birth to Uranus (Sky), to the sea (Pontus), and to the mountains, and she is the mother of the Titans (with Uranus) [S1]. In myth she is also the avenger: she impregnates herself and bears the giant Typhon (or, in the Theogony, the monstrous Typhaon) in revenge for Uranus's mutilation by Cronus, and it is her counsel that sets Cronus against Uranus [S1][S5]. Cultically Gaia/Ge was venerated as the earth-mother at many sites; 'Gaia' is often the generic 'earth' while 'Ge' the deity [S6].
cards.image_credit: Gaia (Roman) · Walters Art Museum · Public domain

cards.name: Uranus
cards.flavor: Sky, the first 'god' and husband of Gaia; father of the Titans. He was overthrown and castrated by his son Cronus.
cards.long: Ouranos (Uranus) is Sky in Hesiod: he loved Gaia and covered her entirely, and their union produced the twelve Titans, the Cyclopes, and the three Hecatoncheires (Hundred-Hands) [S1]. Fearing his monstrous children, Ouranos imprisoned them in Tartarus, and Gaia, grieving and plotting, forged a flint sickle and set her son Cronus to castrate and overthrow him [S1]. Dismembered, his severed parts fell to earth and gave rise to further beings (the Erinyes from his blood, Aphrodite from his severed member, in one account) [S1]. He then retreated to the heavens, and Cronus took his place as the supreme ruler [S1][S5].

cards.name: Cronus
cards.flavor: Titan king who overthrew his father Ouranos and, in turn, was overthrown by his son Zeus.
cards.long: Cronus is the youngest and last of the Titans, and the one Gaia chose to overthrow Ouranos with the flint sickle [S1]. He castrated his father and, with Rhea, reigned over the next age of the world [S1]. Warned by a prophecy (delivered by his parents) that he too would be overthrown by a child, Cronus swallowed each of his newborn children — Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, and Poseidon — as they were born [S1][S5]. Rhea hid the infant Zeus in a Cretan cave, and Zeus, grown, forced Cronus to disgorge his siblings, then led them (with the help of the Cyclopes and Hecatoncheires) to war against the Titans: the Titanomachy [S1]. Defeated, Cronus and the other Titans were cast into Tartarus, with the Hecatoncheires set as guards [S1].
cards.image_credit: Cronus/Saturn · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Rhea
cards.flavor: Titaness, wife of Cronus, mother of the first Olympians; she hid Zeus from her husband.
cards.long: Rhea is a Titaness, daughter of Gaia and Ouranos, and the wife of her brother Cronus [S1]. Mother of the first generation of Olympians, she was the one who saved Zeus: when Cronus was devouring their children, Rhea hid the newborn Zeus in a cave on Crete, and gave Cronus a stone wrapped in swaddling-clothes to swallow in his place [S1][S5]. This act preserved the line that would overthrow Cronus in the Titanomachy [S1].
cards.image_credit: Rhea/Cybele statue · Eleusis Archaeological Museum · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Zeus
cards.flavor: King of the gods, ruler of Olympus, lord of sky, thunder, and kingly order — father of many gods and heroes.
cards.long: Zeus is the supreme god of the classical Greek pantheon, king of Olympus and lord of the sky, thunder, weather, and the moral and political order [S1][S2][S3]. Son of the Titans Cronus and Rhea, he survived his father's attempt to devour him, grew up hidden in Crete, and led the overthrow of the Titans in the Titanomachy, for which he was awarded the sky and the thunderbolt (won from the Cyclopes, who forged it) [S1]. The cosmos was divided by lot: Zeus took the sky, Poseidon the sea, Hades the underworld [S1]. Zeus is the patron of hospitality (xenia), oaths, and kingship, and enforces cosmic order; his many offspring include Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Hermes, Dionysus, and the hero Perseus, among others [S2][S4][S5]. Cultically he was worshipped at Dodona, Olympia, and countless other sites; Zeus was 'the one who gives the season' and the upholder of the world's balance [S6].
cards.image_credit: Bronze Statuette of Zeus (Jupiter) · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain (Met Open Access)

cards.name: Hera
cards.flavor: Queen of the gods, wife of Zeus, goddess of marriage and the protection of women and kings.
cards.long: Hera is the queen of Olympus and Zeus's wife (and, in Hesiod, his sister) [S1]. Goddess of marriage, the family, and the protection of women, she is also the protector of kings and their authority — her wrath, famously, falls on those who dishonor the institution of marriage [S2][S3]. In the Iliad her long resentment of Zeus's many affairs drives much of the plot, and she takes the side of the Greeks [S2]. Her sacred animals include the peacock and the cow (Io, a maiden she transformed into a heifer, is her most famous victim-turned-cow) [S2][S5]. Hera was worshipped at Argos, Samos, and elsewhere; the Heraion at Samos was one of the great sanctuaries [S6].
cards.image_credit: Hera (Ephesus-Vienna type) · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · CC BY-SA 2.0

cards.name: Hades
cards.flavor: God and ruler of the underworld, lord of the dead and of the wealth of the earth; he seized Persephone to be his queen.
cards.long: Hades (the Roman Pluto) is the god and king of the underworld, the realm of the dead [S2][S3]. One of the first-born sons of Cronus and Rhea, he was swallowed at birth and later disgorged by Zeus [S1]. When the world was divided, Hades received the third of it: the underworld [S1]. His most defining act is the seizure of Persephone (daughter of Demeter) to be his queen, which set in motion the myth of the seasons [S4][S5]. Though often conflated with his realm, Hades is a distinct deity: a stern, just, and not especially evil ruler of the dead, who rarely leaves his domain [S2][S3][S5]. The name 'Hades' came to mean the place itself (the underworld) as well as its god — a shift the sources make clear [S2].
cards.image_credit: Terracotta Fragment of a Votive Relief: Hades and Persephone · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain (Met Open Access)

cards.name: Poseidon
cards.flavor: God of the sea, earthquakes, and horses; brother and rival of Zeus, and rival of Athena for Athens.
cards.long: Poseidon (Neptune) is the god of the sea, of earthquakes (he was 'the Earth-shaker'), and of horses — the animals he is said to have created [S1][S2]. Brother of Zeus and Hades, he received the sea when the world was divided [S1]. His rivalry with Zeus for supremacy runs through much of the Iliad, where he is a major (though restrained) actor [S2]. He contested Athena for the patronage of the city that bears his rival's name: he struck the rock and sent forth a salt spring (or, in some accounts, a horse); Athena gave the olive tree, and the city chose her [S5][S6]. He is a father of many — to gods, heroes (e.g. the hero Theseus's divine father is Poseidon in one tradition), and sea-creatures; his most famous confrontation with a mortal is his blinding of Odysseus's son Telegonos and his anger at the blinding of his son the Cyclops Polyphemus by Odysseus [S3].
cards.image_credit: Bronze Statuette of Poseidon (Neptune) · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain (Met Open Access)

cards.name: Athena
cards.flavor: Goddess of wisdom, strategic war, and craft; born fully-formed from Zeus's head; patron of Athens.
cards.long: Athena is the goddess of wisdom, strategic warfare, and craft (crafts of the city, weaving, and the arts) [S1][S2][S4]. She is born in a remarkable and unique way: from the head of Zeus, fully grown and armored, after Zeus swallowed her mother Metis (the goddess of cunning) when pregnant, on the advice that their child would surpass him [S1][S4][S5]. (In the Theogony her mother is Metis; the Iliad names her mother as Metis too, though a variant gives Dione — a minor discrepancy we note.) [S1][S2] She is the patron deity of Athens (the Parthenon was her temple), and her rivalry with Poseidon over the city's patronage is one of the founding myths of Athens — she gave the olive tree and won [S5][S6]. She is the protector of heroes (Odysseus, Perseus, Theseus, Odysseus's son Telemachus), and she is associated with reason, law, and the city-state (polis) [S2][S3][S6].
cards.image_credit: Marble Head and Torso of Athena · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain (Met Open Access)

cards.name: Apollo
cards.flavor: God of the sun (in later association), music, poetry, prophecy, medicine, and archery; twin of Artemis.
cards.long: Apollo is a god of many domains, and his identity shifted across the Greek world: earliest a god associated with light, youth, and the archery, he came to be strongly identified with the sun (a Hellenistic development — the 'sun-god' Apollo is later than the archer Apollo) [S4][S5]. He is the god of music (lyre), poetry (the Muse-calling), prophecy (his oracle at Delphi, the Pythia), medicine (his son Asclepius), and archery [S4][S5][S6]. He is the twin brother of Artemis, and both are children of Zeus and Leto (Latona) [S4]. As a child he slew the Python that guarded the Delphic oracle, founding his sanctuary there [S4][S5]. He is also a god of plague (he sent the arrow-plague on the Greeks in the Iliad's opening) and of its healing — a duality the sources preserve [S2][S4].
cards.image_credit: Apollo of the Belvedere · Vatican Museums · CC BY-SA 3.0

cards.name: Artemis
cards.flavor: Goddess of the hunt, wild animals, and (in later association) the moon; twin of Apollo; protector of young women.
cards.long: Artemis (Diana) is the goddess of the hunt, wild animals, and the wilderness, and the protector of young girls and of childbirth (she is a midwife-goddess in some cults) [S4][S5][S6]. Twin of Apollo, daughter of Zeus and Leto, she asked Zeus for eternal virginity and for the gifts of the hunt [S4][S5]. In later (Hellenistic/Roman) association she was linked to the moon (a development parallel to Apollo's link to the sun) [S4][S5]. She is a powerful, sometimes vengeful goddess: Actaeon was turned into a stag and torn by his own hounds for seeing her bathing; Orion was punished for his arrogance; Arachne was transformed for her hubristic weaving [S4][S5]. Her great sanctuary was at Ephesus (the Temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders) and at Brauron in Attica [S6].
cards.image_credit: Artemis of Ephesus · Musei Capitolini, Rome · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Ares
cards.flavor: God of the violent, bloodier aspect of war; son of Zeus and Hera; lover of Aphrodite.
cards.long: Ares (Mars) is the god of war — specifically its violent, brutal, blood-soaked aspect, as opposed to Athena's strategic, disciplined side of war [S2][S4]. Son of Zeus and Hera, he is one of the few Olympians born of a union that required no pregnancy in the usual sense (Hera 'conceived' him, in one account, without a consort) [S4][S5]. He is a major character in the Iliad, where he is a fierce combatant but is also treated with a mix of awe and disdain — the Greeks call him 'the hound of war' [S2]. His most famous myth is his affair with Aphrodite, caught in the act by her husband Hephaestus and displayed before the assembled gods in shame [S2][S5].
cards.image_credit: "Ludovisi Ares" · Palazzo Altemps, Rome · Public domain

cards.name: Aphrodite
cards.flavor: Goddess of love, beauty, and desire; born (in the Theogony) from the sea-foam around a severed divine member.
cards.long: Aphrodite (Venus) is the goddess of love, beauty, desire, and sexual love [S1][S4][S5]. Her birth is one of the great variants in Greek myth: in Hesiod's Theogony she is born from the sea-foam that gathered around the severed member of Ouranos (cast into the sea by Cronus), rising fully formed at Cythera [S1]; in the Iliad she is the daughter of Zeus and Dione [S2]. Both accounts are preserved and the difference is genuine [S1][S2]. She is married to Hephaestus (the smith-god) but famously lovers with Ares; her children include Eros (Love) and, with Ares, Phobos (Fear) and Deimos (Dread) [S4][S5]. The Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite opens with her power over gods and mortals alike [S4].
cards.image_credit: Limestone Statue of Aphrodite Holding Winged Eros · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain (Met Open Access)

cards.name: Hermes
cards.flavor: Messenger of the gods, god of travelers, commerce, and thieves; guide of souls to the underworld (psychopomp).
cards.long: Hermes (Mercury) is the messenger of the gods and the god of a remarkably wide range of activities: travelers, commerce, cattle, thievery (he is the divine patron of cunning and the 'trickster'), and the boundary (he is Hermes 'the guide' at crossroads) [S1][S2][S4][S5]. Son of Zeus and the nymph Maia, he is a child-prodigy: on the day of his birth he stole Apollo's cattle and invented the lyre from a tortoise shell, then traded it to Apollo [S4][S5]. His most solemn role is as psychopomp — the guide who leads the souls of the dead to the underworld (he escorts Persephone, he guides Odysseus's crew's dead, etc.) [S3][S4]. He is the patron of thieves, merchants, and travelers, and his wand (the caduceus, winged and entwined by two serpents) is his signature [S4][S5].
cards.image_credit: Marble Statue of Hermes (after Polykleitos) · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain (Met Open Access)

cards.name: Dionysus
cards.flavor: God of wine, ecstasy, theater, and fertility; the only Olympian born of a mortal mother (Semele).
cards.long: Dionysus (Bacchus) is the god of wine, vine, ecstasy, theater, and fertility — a liminal, dual-natured god whose festivals (the Dionysia) were central to Athenian civic and religious life [S4][S5][S6]. He is the only Olympian born of a mortal mother: his mother Semele, a mortal princess, was persuaded by Hera to demand proof of Zeus's divinity (a bolt of lightning), and was destroyed by it; Zeus saved the unborn child by sewing him into his thigh until he was ready to be born [S5]. (This is the standard account; a variant gives a double birth.) [S5] He is the patron of the theater — the great tragedy and comedy festivals at Athens were in his honor [S6]. He is a god of transformation and ecstasy, and his followers (the Maenads) are in a state of divine frenzy [S5][S6].
cards.image_credit: Dionysus torso · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · CC0

cards.name: Hephaestus
cards.flavor: God of fire and the forge, the divine smith who made the gods' weapons; married to Aphrodite.
cards.long: Hephaestus (Vulcan) is the god of fire, the forge, and craft — the divine blacksmith who made the gods' finest weapons and treasures, including Zeus's thunderbolt and his own net that caught Ares and Aphrodite [S1][S2][S4][S5]. His parentage is a genuine variant: in the Iliad he is the son of Hera alone (Hera, spurned by Zeus, produced him without a consort, in a fit of spite); in the Theogony he is the son of Zeus and Hera [S1][S2]. He is lame (in one account he was thrown from Olympus by Zeus and crippled in the fall) and dwells in an underground forge, often associated with volcanoes [S2][S4][S5]. Despite his ugliness and lameness, he is the only god who can match Zeus in craft, and he is married to the beautiful Aphrodite (a union that is itself a source of myth, given her affair with Ares) [S2][S4][S5].
cards.image_credit: Athena and Hephaestus · British Museum · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Demeter
cards.flavor: Goddess of the harvest and the grain; mother of Persephone; her grief at Persephone's abduction set the seasons in motion.
cards.long: Demeter (Ceres) is the goddess of the harvest, the grain, and the fertility of the earth [S1][S4][S5]. One of the first-born children of Cronus and Rhea (swallowed and later disgorged by Zeus), she is the mother of Persephone [S4][S5]. Her defining myth is the abduction of Persephone by Hades: in her grief, Demeter withdrew the fertility of the earth, and the world went cold and barren until a compromise was reached — Persephone would spend part of the year with her mother (spring/summer) and part in the underworld (autumn/winter), giving rise to the cycle of the seasons [S4][S5]. Her great sanctuary was at Eleusis, where the Eleusinian Mysteries (a secret initiation cult) were held in her and Persephone's honor [S6].
cards.image_credit: Relief Fragments from the Great Eleusinian Relief · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain (Met Open Access)

cards.name: Persephone
cards.flavor: Queen of the underworld, wife of Hades, daughter of Demeter; her annual return to earth gives spring.
cards.long: Persephone (Proserpina) is the daughter of Demeter and Zeus, and the queen of the underworld as wife of Hades [S4][S5]. Her story is the founding myth of the seasons: Hades abducts her (in some accounts she is plucking flowers in a meadow) to be his queen; Demeter's grief withholds the earth's fertility; a compromise is reached whereby Persephone spends part of the year (the warmer months) on earth with her mother and part (the colder months) in the underworld with Hades [S4][S5]. The detail that made the arrangement binding: while in the underworld she ate six pomegranate seeds, and so was bound to return to the dead for a portion of each year [S4][S5]. She is both a spring/vegetation goddess and the queen of the dead — a dual role the sources preserve without resolving the tension [S4][S6].
cards.image_credit: Terracotta Fragment of a Votive Relief: Hades and Persephone · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain (Met Open Access)

cards.name: Hestia
cards.flavor: Goddess of the hearth and the home, the eldest of the Olympians; she renounced a seat on Olympus to let Zeus divide the world.
cards.long: Hestia is the goddess of the hearth, the home, and the domestic flame — the eldest of the first-born children of Cronus and Rhea [S1][S5]. She is a serene, non-combative deity, and in one famous account she renounced her place among the twelve Olympians, yielding her seat so that the world could be divided (or so that Dionysus could take it) [S5]. Her cult was the first sacrifice offered at the opening of any public gathering, and the hearth (hearth-fire) was the center of the Greek home and the city [S6]. She is a figure of domestic stability and continuity rather than dramatic myth.
cards.image_credit: Hestia Giustiniani · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Leto
cards.flavor: Titaness, mother of Apollo and Artemis by Zeus.
cards.long: Leto (Latona) is a Titaness, daughter of Coeus and Phoebe, and the mother of Apollo and Artemis by Zeus [S1][S4]. She is a relatively minor figure in the myths but central as the mother of the twin gods. Her pregnancy was pursued by Hera's jealousy (she was barred from giving birth on the dry land of the earth, and gave birth on the floating island of Delos) [S4][S5].

cards.name: Metis
cards.flavor: Titaness of counsel and cunning; mother of Athena; swallowed by Zeus, from whose head Athena was born.
cards.long: Metis is a Titaness, the personification of counsel and cunning, and the first wife of Zeus [S1][S4][S5]. A prophecy said that their child would overthrow Zeus as he had overthrown Cronus, so Zeus swallowed Metis while she was pregnant with Athena; Athena was then born fully formed from Zeus's head [S1][S4][S5]. Metis is thus the mother of Athena and a symbol of the cunning wisdom that Zeus embodies.

cards.name: Perseus
cards.flavor: Hero who slew the Gorgon Medusa and rescued Andromeda; aided by Athena, Hermes, and the gift of winged sandals.
cards.long: Perseus is the hero who slew the Gorgon Medusa and rescued the maiden Andromeda from the sea-monster Cetus [S4][S5]. Son of Zeus and the Danaid Danaë, he was sent to fetch Medusa's head by the tyrant Polydectes; aided by Athena (who gave him a mirror-shield), Hermes (who gave him winged sandals and a sickle), and the Naiads, he beheaded Medusa — and from her blood sprang the winged horse Pegasus [S5]. He then rescued Andromeda, who was being offered to Cetus, and took her as his wife [S5]. Perseus is one of the canonical Greek heroes, and his story is a model of the divinely-aided hero.
cards.image_credit: Bronze Mirror with Perseus and the Graiai · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain (Met Open Access)

cards.name: Medusa
cards.flavor: The Gorgon with snakes for hair whose gaze turned viewers to stone; slain by Perseus.
cards.long: Medusa is one of the three Gorgon sisters (with Stheno and Euryale), and the only one who was mortal; her hair was living snakes and her gaze turned any who met it to stone [S4][S5]. In the standard account (Ovid, building on earlier tradition) she was a beautiful maiden transformed into a monster (in Ovid, for her hubris and for an offense against Athena), and she was slain by Perseus, who used Athena's mirror-shield to avoid meeting her gaze [S5]. (In Hesiod's earlier Theogony the Gorgons are monstrous from the start, daughters of the sea-gods Phorcys and Ceto — the 'beautiful maiden' version is later, from Ovid.) [S1][S5] From her severed neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus and the giant Chrysaor [S1][S5].
cards.image_credit: Gilded Silver Relief: Woman, Herakles, Artemis, and a Gorgon · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Public domain (Met Open Access)

cards.name: Typhon
cards.flavor: The greatest of the monsters, born of Gaia to avenge the Titans; he was the only being to seriously wound Zeus before being overthrown.
cards.long: Typhon (Typhoeus) is the greatest and most terrifying of the Greek monsters, a hundred-headed (in some accounts) offspring of Gaia, born (in the Theogony, in a passage widely judged to be a later interpolation) to avenge the defeat of the Titans [S1]. He warred against the gods and was the only creature to seriously wound Zeus (who was cut and whose sinews were cut, causing him to fall) before Zeus recovered, regained his thunderbolt, and buried Typhon under Mount Etna — whose fires are explained as Typhon's breathing [S1][S5]. He is the father (with the monster Echidna) of many of the great monsters of Greek myth, including Cerberus, the Hydra, and the Chimera [S1][S5].
cards.image_credit: Typhon · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Cerberus
cards.flavor: The three-headed hound that guards the gates of the underworld, preventing the dead from leaving.
cards.long: Cerberus is the three-headed hound that guards the gates of the underworld, preventing the dead from leaving and the living from entering unbidden [S1][S3][S5]. Son of the monsters Typhon and Echidna (and sibling to the Hydra and the Chimera), he is one of the great 'impossible' creatures of Greek myth [S1][S5]. His capture is the final (twelfth) labor of Heracles, who wrestled him down and brought him to the surface without killing him [S5].

cards.name: Heracles
cards.flavor: The greatest of the Greek heroes, son of Zeus; he performed the twelve labors and was raised to Olympus.
cards.long: Heracles (Hercules) is the greatest of the Greek heroes, the son of Zeus and the mortal Alcmena [S2][S5]. Driven to madness by Hera (who resented Zeus's affair with Alcmena) he killed his own children, and was later set to perform the twelve labors by King Eurystheus as penance — including capturing Cerberus, slaying the Nemean lion, and capturing the Cretan bull [S5]. After his death (he was burned on a pyre, set up by his wife or by fate), he was raised to Olympus and married the goddess Hebe [S5]. He is the model of the strength-hero, and his cult was widespread; he was a patron of athletes and of the city of Thebes (his birthplace) [S6].
cards.image_credit: Heracles approaching seated Zeus and Hera · National Archaeological Museum, Athens · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Odysseus
cards.flavor: The cunning king of Ithaca, hero of the Odyssey; his ten-year journey home from Troy is a foundational epic.
cards.long: Odysseus (Ulysses) is the king of Ithaca and the hero of Homer's Odyssey — the epic of his ten-year journey home from the Trojan War [S3]. A man of extraordinary cunning (his name is associated with 'metis,' cunning intelligence), he devised the Wooden Horse that won the Trojans the war [S2][S3], and he overcame a succession of monsters and gods on his way home: the Cyclops Polyphemus (whom he blinded and outwitted, calling himself 'Nobody'), the witch Circe, the Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, and the cattle of the sun [S3]. His defining qualities are wit, endurance, and the desire to return home (nostos) to his wife Penelope and son Telemachus [S3].
cards.image_credit: Odysseus blinding Polyphemus · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Maia
cards.flavor: Nymph, daughter of the Titan Atlas, and mother of Hermes by Zeus.
cards.long: Maia is a nymph, one of the Pleiades (daughters of the Titan Atlas and the oceanid Pleione), and the mother of Hermes by Zeus [S1][S4][S5]. She is a minor figure, known chiefly as Hermes's mother; the Homeric Hymn to Hermes opens with her nursing the infant god in a cave [S4].
cards.image_credit: Coin of Pheneos showing the head of Maia · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Atlas
cards.flavor: Titan condemned to hold up the sky (or the heavens) for eternity; father of the Pleiades.
cards.long: Atlas is a Titan, son of Iapetus, who was punished by Zeus after the Titanomachy for siding with the Titans; he was condemned to hold up the sky (or the heavens) on his shoulders for eternity [S1][S5]. He is the father (with the oceanid Pleione) of the Pleiades, a group of sisters who were turned into stars [S1][S5]. He is also the father of the Hesperides and, in some accounts, of the Gorgons' mother Ceto. The 'holding up the sky' image is a later (post-Homeric) development; the earliest Atlas is a great Titan of strength [S5].
cards.image_credit: Atlas with celestial sphere (Farnese Atlas) · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · CC BY-SA 2.0

cards.name: Danae
cards.flavor: Mortal princess, daughter of King Acrisius of Argos; mother of Perseus by Zeus.
cards.long: Danaë is a mortal princess, daughter of King Acrisius of Argos. When an oracle warned Acrisius that he would be overthrown by his grandson, he imprisoned Danaë in a bronze tower to prevent her from bearing a child. Zeus came to her (in the form of a shower of gold) and she bore Perseus [S5]. Acrisius later cast mother and son out in a chest, but they were saved; Perseus went on to become the hero who slew Medusa [S5].

cards.name: Semele
cards.flavor: Mortal princess, mother of Dionysus by Zeus; destroyed by a bolt of lightning, from whose womb Zeus saved the unborn god.
cards.long: Semele is a mortal princess (daughter of Cadmus of Thebes) who became the mistress of Zeus and bore him Dionysus. Hera, jealous, persuaded Semele to demand that Zeus prove his divinity by appearing to her in his full glory (a bolt of lightning); the mortal mother was destroyed by the lightning, but Zeus saved the unborn child by sewing it into his thigh until it was ready to be born [S5]. Semele's story is the origin of Dionysus's 'double birth' (first of Semele, then of Zeus).

cards.name: Eros
cards.flavor: God of love and desire; in the Theogony a primordial force, in later myth the son of Aphrodite.
cards.long: Eros (Cupid) is the god of love and desire. In Hesiod's Theogony he is a primordial being, born directly from Chaos — an impersonal force of attraction [S1]; in later myth he is the son of Aphrodite (and in some accounts of Ares), the winged child who drives gods and mortals to love [S4][S5]. The two conceptions coexist: the cosmic force and the charming child-god.
cards.image_credit: Eros (Farnese dolphin group) · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Andromeda
cards.flavor: Princess of Aethiopia, offered to the sea-monster Cetus and rescued by Perseus, who married her.
cards.long: Andromeda is a princess of Aethiopia whose mother Cassiopeia (a queen) boasted that Andromeda was more beautiful than the Nereids; Poseidon sent the monster Cetus to ravage the coast, and Andromeda was chained to a rock as a sacrifice. Perseus, passing by, slew Cetus with the head of Medusa and rescued her, and she became his wife [S5].

cards.name: Echidna
cards.flavor: Half-woman, half-serpent monster who, with Typhon, mothered many of the great monsters of Greek myth.
cards.long: Echidna is a half-woman, half-serpent creature who dwelt in a cave and, in partnership with the monster Typhon, mothered many of the great monsters of Greek myth, including Cerberus, the Lernaean Hydra, the Chimera, the Sphinx, and Orthrus [S1][S5]. She is the 'mother of monsters,' a source of the chthonic terror that the heroes of Greek myth must overcome.

cards.name: Oceanus
cards.flavor: Primordial Titan, personification of the great river that (in Greek thought) encircled the inhabited world.
cards.long: Oceanus is the primordial Titan who personifies the great ocean-river that, in Greek cosmography, encircled the inhabited world (the oikoumene) [S1]. He is the eldest of the Titans and the consort of Tethys; together they are the parents of the rivers, the oceanids, and the winds [S1]. He is a vast, serene figure, more a cosmic boundary than an active god, but his role as the boundary of the world is cosmographically important.
cards.image_credit: Oceanus and Tethys mosaic · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · CC BY-SA 3.0

cards.name: Tethys
cards.flavor: Primordial Titaness, consort of Oceanus and mother of the rivers and oceanids.
cards.long: Tethys is a primordial Titaness, daughter of Gaia and Ouranos, and the consort of her brother Oceanus [S1]. Together they are the parents of the rivers, the oceanids (sea-nymphs), and the winds [S1]. She is a vast, maternal figure associated with the productive waters of the world.
cards.image_credit: Tethys · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Alcmena
cards.flavor: Mortal woman, wife of Amphitryon and mother of Heracles by Zeus.
cards.long: Alcmena is a mortal woman, the wife of Amphitryon, king of Thebes. Zeus took her in the form of Amphitryon and fathered Heracles [S2][S5]. (The 'Amphitryon' story — Zeus impersonating the husband — is a later elaboration; the core fact is that Heracles's divine father is Zeus and his mortal mother is Alcmena.) [S5]

cards.name: Penelope
cards.flavor: Queen of Ithaca, faithful wife of Odysseus; she warded off the suitors for twenty years while her husband was away.
cards.long: Penelope is the wife of Odysseus and queen of Ithaca. During her husband's long absence (first the ten years of the Trojan War, then the ten years of his wanderings), she was besieged by suitors who pressed her to remarry. She delayed them with the ruse of weaving a shroud by day and unwinding it by night, remaining faithful to Odysseus until his return [S3].

cards.name: Telemachus
cards.flavor: Son of Odysseus and Penelope; the Odyssey begins with his quest to find his father.
cards.long: Telemachus is the son of Odysseus and Penelope. The Odyssey opens with him, now a young man, being urged by Athena (in disguise) to take charge and to seek news of his missing father. His journey (the 'telemachy') to Pylos and Sparta to find out what happened to Odysseus frames the epic's opening books [S3].

cards.name: Hebe
cards.flavor: Goddess of youth, cup-bearer of the gods; she married Heracles after his deification.
cards.long: Hebe is the goddess of youth and the cup-bearer of the gods at Olympus. She is the daughter of Zeus and Hera [S5]. After Heracles was raised to Olympus following his death, he married Hebe [S5].

cards.name: Ginnungagap
cards.flavor: The yawning void between fire and ice — the primordial space from which the first beings emerged.
cards.long: Ginnungagap is the 'yawning gap' at the center of Norse creation: Niflheim (ice) lay to the north, Muspelheim (fire) to the south, and between them the void where rime and frost formed [S2]. From this gap, the first living being — the ice-giant Ymir — and the cow Auðhumbla emerged [S1][S2]. Ginnungagap is not a 'place' so much as the primordial condition of the world before it had shape [S2].

cards.name: Muspel (fire)
cards.flavor: The realm of fire to the south, whose heat began the creation of the world.
cards.long: Muspelheim is the realm of fire, to the south of Ginnungagap. Its sparks and heat dripped onto the rime of Niflheim, melting it and beginning the creation of the world [S2]. At Ragnarök, Muspel's fire (led by Surt) destroys the world [S1][S2].

cards.name: Niflheim (ice)
cards.flavor: The realm of ice and mist to the north, source of the rime that became Ymir.
cards.long: Niflheim is the realm of ice and mist, to the north of Ginnungagap. Its rivers (the Élivágar) flowed with rime, and where the rime met the heat of Muspelheim, Ymir and Auðhumbla formed [S2].

cards.name: Ymir
cards.flavor: The first being, an ice-giant formed from the rime of Ginnungagap; his body became the world.
cards.long: Ymir is the first living being, a giant of rime and frost who formed in Ginnungagap and was nourished by the milk of the cow Auðhumbla, who licked him free of the ice [S2]. From his sweating armpits came two more giants (a male and a female), and from his foot a six-headed son [S2]. When the gods Odin, Vili, and Vé killed Ymir, his body became the world: his blood the seas, his flesh the earth, his bones the mountains, his skull the sky, and his brains the clouds [S2]. Ymir's descendants, the frost-giants (jötnar), are the gods' chief enemies [S1][S2].

cards.name: Auðhumbla
cards.flavor: The primordial cow who licked Ymir free of the ice and whose milk nourished him.
cards.long: Auðhumbla is the first cow, formed from the rime of Ginnungagap. She licked the ice free of Ymir's form and nourished him with her milk; from the salt she licked from the ice came the first god, Búri [S2]. Auðhumbla is a creature of the primordial world, not a god.

cards.name: Búri
cards.flavor: The first god, formed from the salt the primordial cow licked from the ice; father of Borr.
cards.long: Búri is the first of the gods, formed from the salt that the cow Auðhumbla licked from the ice [S2]. He is the father of Borr, who married the giantess Bestla, and their sons are the three gods Odin, Vili, and Vé [S2]. Búri is a remote ancestor, barely developed in the sources — he is the link between the primordial world and the divine line.

cards.name: Borr
cards.flavor: Son of Búri and husband of the giantess Bestla; father of Odin, Vili, and Vé.
cards.long: Borr is the son of Búri and the husband of the giantess Bestla. Their sons are the three brothers Odin, Vili, and Vé, who created the world from the body of Ymir [S2]. Borr is another remote ancestor, named chiefly to complete the genealogy of the gods.

cards.name: Bestla
cards.flavor: The giantess who married Borr and bore the three gods Odin, Vili, and Vé.
cards.long: Bestla is a giantess (jötun) who married the god Borr and bore the three brothers Odin, Vili, and Vé [S2]. Her giant lineage is significant: it reminds that the gods and the giants share a common ancestry, and that the gods' enemies are also, in a sense, their kin [S2].
domains: the giantess mother of the gods

cards.name: Odin
cards.flavor: The Allfather, chief of the Æsir: god of wisdom, war, death, magic, and poetry. He sacrificed an eye for wisdom and hung on Yggdrasil to win the runes.
cards.long: Odin is the Allfather, chief of the Æsir and the most complex of the Norse gods [S1][S2][S3]. He is the god of wisdom, war, death, magic (seiðr), poetry, and the runes, and the ruler of the hall Valhalla, where he receives the slain warriors (the Einherjar) in preparation for Ragnarök [S2]. To gain wisdom, he sacrificed one of his eyes to the well-being Mímir [S2]; to win the runes, he hung himself on the world-tree Yggdrasil for nine nights, pierced by his own spear [S1]. His two ravens, Huginn (Thought) and Muninn (Memory), fly over the world each day and report to him; his two wolves, Geri and Freki, and his eight-legged horse Sleipnir are his companions [S2]. Odin is a figure of profound duality: the wise king and the wandering magician, the god of life and the god of death, the allfather and the one who will die to Fenrir at Ragnarök [S1][S2]. He is the patron of the skalds and of the poetic art, and his name is associated with the 'Odinic' trance (the 'Riding Out,' or hamingja) [S3].
cards.image_credit: Odin, der Göttervater (Odin, the Father of the Gods) · Romantic-era illustration (widely reproduced) · Public domain

cards.name: Vili
cards.flavor: One of the three brothers (with Odin and Vé) who created the world from Ymir's body. Barely developed in the sources.
cards.long: Vili is one of the three brothers — Odin, Vili, and Vé — sons of Borr and Bestla, who together created the world from the body of the giant Ymir [S2]. After the creation, Vili (and Vé) largely disappear from the myths; Odin becomes the chief god, and the 'three brothers' are mostly a memory of the creation act [S2]. Vili is one of the 'thin' figures of Norse myth — named, but not developed.
domains: one of the three brothers who made the world

cards.name: Vé
cards.flavor: One of the three brothers (with Odin and Vili) who created the world. Barely developed in the sources.
cards.long: Vé is the third of the three brothers — Odin, Vili, and Vé — who created the world from Ymir's body [S2]. Like Vili, he is named in the creation but then largely absent from the myths [S2].
domains: one of the three brothers who made the world

cards.name: Thor
cards.flavor: God of thunder and storms, wielder of the hammer Mjölnir, and the mightiest protector of the gods and of humans.
cards.long: Thor is the god of thunder and the mightiest of the Æsir, the protector of the gods and of humanity [S1][S2][S3]. His weapon is the hammer Mjölnir, which never misses and which he uses against the giants and the monsters that threaten the world [S2]. He is the son of Odin and of a giantess (Járnsaxa in one account, the earth in another) [S2]. Thor is a god of the common people — his hammer was a symbol of protection worn by ordinary people, and his name is the source of 'Thursday' (Thor's day) [S3][S4]. His enemies are the giants (jötnar) and the great monsters: the world-serpent Jörmungandr, whom he will slay (and be slain by) at Ragnarök, and the giant Hrungnir, whom he fells with Mjölnir [S1][S2]. He is a figure of raw, protective strength — not the subtle wisdom of Odin, but the brute force that keeps the world safe [S2][S3].
cards.image_credit: Thor's Battle Against the Jötnar · National Museum, Stockholm · Public domain

cards.name: Frigg
cards.flavor: Queen of the Æsir, wife of Odin, mother of Baldr; a goddess of marriage and the home.
cards.long: Frigg is the queen of the Æsir, the wife of Odin, and the mother of Baldr [S2]. She is a goddess of marriage, the home, and (in some accounts) the sky. Her most defining myth is the death of Baldr: when she learned that her son was fated to die, she extracted oaths from all things not to harm him — except the mistletoe, which she overlooked (or refused to bind); Loki then exploited this to kill Baldr [S2]. Frigg is a figure of maternal grief and of the limits of divine power — she cannot save her son [S2].
cards.image_credit: The Oseberg Ship · Viking Ship Museum, Oslo (Vikingskipshuset) · Public domain

cards.name: Baldr
cards.flavor: The brightest and most beloved of the gods, associated with light and purity; his murder by Loki (via the mistletoe) is the great tragedy of Norse myth.
cards.long: Baldr is the brightest, fairest, and most beloved of the gods, associated with light and (in some accounts) with the sun [S1][S2]. He and his wife Nanna live in the hall of Breidablik [S2]. His death is the great tragedy of Norse myth: his mother Frigg, warned of his fate, extracted oaths from all things not to harm him — except the mistletoe, which she overlooked; Loki, disguised as an old woman, learned of this and guided Baldr's blind brother Höðr to throw a mistletoe dart at him, killing him [S2]. Baldr's death is the beginning of the end: it is the act that sets the chain of events leading to Ragnarök in motion [S1][S2]. His son is Fosite (Forsétir), god of peace and reconciliation [S2].
cards.image_credit: The Death of Balder (Balders Død) · Danish rococo painting · Public domain

cards.name: Höðr
cards.flavor: The blind brother of Baldr, who unknowingly threw the mistletoe dart that killed his brother, at Loki's instigation.
cards.long: Höðr is the blind brother of Baldr. At Loki's instigation (disguised as an old woman), Höðr was led to throw a mistletoe dart at Baldr, killing him [S2]. Höðr is a figure of tragic innocence — he did not know what he was doing, and he is the unwitting instrument of the great tragedy [S2].
cards.image_credit: Höðr · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Loki
cards.flavor: The trickster god — part of the Æsir but not a true god — who engineered Baldr's death and will fight the gods at Ragnarök.
cards.long: Loki is the trickster of Norse myth — a figure of cunning, transformation, and disruption. He is 'blood-related' to the gods (son of the giant Fárbauti in one account) but is not a true Æsir; he is a complex, ambiguous figure who helps the gods (he wins Sif's hair, the ship Skidblaðnir, and Thor's hammer, all through trickery) and who also destroys them (he engineers Baldr's death and will lead the enemies at Ragnarök) [S1][S2]. His children are among the greatest threats to the world: the wolf Fenrir (who will kill Odin), the world-serpent Jörmungandr (who will kill Thor), and Hel (who rules the realm of the dead) [S2]. At Ragnarök, Loki fights against the gods and is ultimately caught by the river-vine and slain by the serpent's poison [S1][S2]. Loki is the great ambivalent figure: helper and destroyer, the one who holds the fate of the world in his cunning [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Loki leaves the hall and threatens the Æsir with fire · Danish mythological illustration · Public domain

cards.name: Týr
cards.flavor: God of war, justice, and law; he sacrificed his hand to bind the wolf Fenrir.
cards.long: Týr is the god of war, justice, and law, and (in some accounts) of the sky. His defining act is the binding of the wolf Fenrir: the gods tricked Fenrir into letting them bind him, but only Týr was brave enough to place his hand in the wolf's mouth as a pledge of good faith; when the binding held, Fenrir bit off his hand [S2]. Týr is thus the god of the sacrifice of justice — he gave his hand to keep a promise, and he is the patron of oaths and of the law [S2]. His name gives 'Tuesday' (Tiw's day) [S3].
cards.image_credit: Tyr and Fenrir · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Freyr
cards.flavor: God of fertility, peace, and the sea, of the Vanir; he gives his sword to a dwarf and is slain by Surt at Ragnarök.
cards.long: Freyr is a god of the Vanir (a second divine tribe), associated with fertility, peace, the sun (in some accounts), and the sea [S2]. He owns the ship Skíðblaðnir (which folds up to fit in a pocket) and the boar Gullinbursti, and he is the one who gives a sword that fights by itself to a dwarf [S2]. His tragedy: to win the giantess Gerðr, he gives away his magic sword — and at Ragnarök, he is forced to fight Surt the fire-giant without it, and is slain [S1][S2]. Freyr is a god of peace and plenty, whose loss of his weapon is the price of his love [S2].
cards.image_credit: The Gokstad Ship · Viking Ship Museum, Oslo (Vikingskipshuset) · CC BY-SA 3.0

cards.name: Freyja
cards.flavor: Goddess of love, beauty, fertility, war, and magic (seiðr), of the Vanir; she receives half of the slain in her hall Fólkvangr.
cards.long: Freyja is a goddess of the Vanir, associated with love, beauty, fertility, war, and the magic of seiðr [S2]. She is the sister of Freyr and the owner of the necklace Brísingamen [S2]. She is a war-goddess: she chooses half of the slain for her hall Fólkvangr (the other half going to Odin's Valhalla) [S2]. She is also a goddess of seiðr (a form of Norse magic), which was associated with both power and taboo [S2]. Freyrja is a complex, powerful female deity who straddles the domains of love and war [S2].
cards.image_credit: Freyja and the Necklace (Brísingamen) · British romantic-era illustration · Public domain

cards.name: Njord
cards.flavor: God of the sea, calm winds, and wealth, of the Vanir; father of Freyr and Freyja.
cards.long: Njord is a god of the Vanir, associated with the sea, calm winds, wealth, and sailing [S2]. He is the father of Freyr and Freyja [S2]. His home is Nóatún (the boat-stall), by the sea [S2]. Njord is a god of the practical, maritime aspects of life — the calm sea, the good wind, the wealth that comes from the sea [S2].

cards.name: Heimdall
cards.flavor: The watchman of the gods, who guards the Bifrost and will sound the horn Gjallarhorn at Ragnarök; he and Loki will kill each other.
cards.long: Heimdall is the watchman of the gods, the one who guards the Bifrost (the rainbow bridge to Asgard) and who can see and hear across the whole world [S2]. He is the god of the light and the dawn, and he will sound the horn Gjallarhorn to wake the gods at Ragnarök [S1][S2]. At the final battle, Heimdall and Loki will fight and kill each other [S1][S2]. His parentage is a genuine variant: in one account he is the son of Odin and of a giantess named Angrboða (which is odd, because Angrboða is elsewhere Loki's wife); in another he has nine mothers [S2].
cards.image_credit: Wooden statue of Heimdall · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Víðarr
cards.flavor: The silent son of Odin, who will avenge his father by slaying the wolf Fenrir at Ragnarök.
cards.long: Víðarr is the son of Odin and (in one account) of the giantess Gríðr; he is a god of silence and of strength. At Ragnarök, he will avenge his father by slaying the wolf Fenrir, who has killed Odin, by kicking the wolf's lower jaw up and driving his sword through its head [S1][S2]. Víðarr is the 'silent' god — he speaks little, and his vengeance is the only one that succeeds at Ragnarök [S2].
cards.image_credit: Víðarr · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Váli
cards.flavor: The son of Odin, who will avenge his brother Baldr by slaying Höðr.
cards.long: Váli is the son of Odin, born (in one account) from the body of Baldr after his death, to avenge him. At the funeral of Baldr, Váli will slay Höðr, the blind brother who killed Baldr [S2]. Váli is a figure of swift, one-act vengeance — he exists to kill Höðr and then disappears from the myths [S2].

cards.name: Fenrir
cards.flavor: The great wolf, son of Loki, whom the gods bound with the magic ribbon Gleipnir; he will kill Odin at Ragnarök.
cards.long: Fenrir is the great wolf, son of Loki and the giantess Angerboa (Angrboða) [S2]. As a pup he was raised in Asgard, but the gods grew afraid of his strength and tried to bind him. The first two bindings (Leadbond and Dromi) he broke, but the third — a magic ribbon made of six impossible things (Gleipnir) — held, because only Týr placed his hand in the wolf's mouth as a pledge; when the binding held, Fenrir bit off his hand [S2]. Fenrir will break free at Ragnarök and grow so large that his jaw touches the earth and his mouth the sky; he will swallow the sun and kill Odin, who will be avenged by his son Víðarr [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Odin and Fenris · British illustration · Public domain

cards.name: Jörmungandr
cards.flavor: The world-serpent, son of Loki, whom the gods cast into the sea; he encircles the world and will kill Thor at Ragnarök.
cards.long: Jörmungandr (the Midgard Serpent) is the world-serpent, son of Loki and Angerboa [S2]. The gods, fearing him, cast him into the sea around Midgard, where he grew so large that he encircles the whole world and bites his own tail [S2]. Thor famously fishes him up in one episode (the great catch), but lets him go when he realizes the serpent's size [S2]. At Ragnarök, Jörmungandr rises from the sea, and Thor slays him — but walks nine steps and dies of the serpent's venom [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Thor and the Midgard Serpent (Jörmungandr) · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Hel
cards.flavor: The ruler of the realm of the dead (Hel), daughter of Loki; she is half-living, half-dead.
cards.long: Hel is the daughter of Loki and Angerboa, and the ruler of the realm of the dead (also called Hel) [S2]. She is a strange being: half of her body is living and the other half is corpse-like (the color of a dead fish) [S2]. The gods, wishing to get rid of her, cast her into the north with a hall of the dead, where she rules over those who die of sickness or old age (as opposed to those who die in battle, who go to Valhalla) [S2]. Hel is not 'evil' in the Christian sense; she is the ruler of the dead, a necessary part of the cosmic order [S2].
symbols: half-living, half-dead (half her body is corpse-like)
cards.image_credit: Hel · Russian symbolist painting · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Sleipnir
cards.flavor: The eight-legged horse of Odin, born of Loki (in the form of a mare).
cards.long: Sleipnir is the eight-legged horse of Odin, the only steed that can ride between the worlds [S2]. In the myth of his birth, Loki, in the form of a mare, mated with the stallion Svaðilfari (a giant's horse) and bore Sleipnir [S2]. Sleipnir is grey, eight-legged, and the fastest of horses; he carries Odin between the worlds [S2].
cards.image_credit: Odin on Sleipnir (17th-c. Icelandic manuscript) · National Library of Iceland (Háskólabibliótekin), MS Neustadt 97 · Public domain

cards.name: Angrboða
cards.flavor: The giantess who, with Loki, mothered the great monsters: Fenrir, Jörmungandr, and Hel.
cards.long: Angerboa (Angrboða) is a giantess who, in partnership with Loki, mothered the great monsters of the end of the world: the wolf Fenrir, the world-serpent Jörmungandr, and Hel, the ruler of the dead [S2]. She is the 'mother of monsters,' the source of the threats that will destroy the world at Ragnarök [S2].
domains: the giantess mother of the monsters

cards.name: Sif
cards.flavor: The wife of Thor, whose golden hair was cut off by Loki and regrown by dwarves as real gold.
cards.long: Sif is the wife of Thor and the mother of Ullr (in some accounts). Her defining myth: Loki, in a fit of mischief, cut off her beautiful golden hair; Thor threatened to kill him, so Loki went to the dwarves and had them make new hair for her — real gold, which grew like real hair [S2]. Sif is a figure of beauty and of the domestic side of the Æsir [S2].
cards.image_credit: Sif · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Ullr
cards.flavor: The archer-god, associated with winter, skiing, and archery; son of Thor.
cards.long: Ullr is a god of the Æsir, associated with archery, skiing, and the winter [S2]. He is the son of Thor and Sif (in some accounts) [S2]. Ullr is a relatively minor figure, but he is the patron of archery and of the winter sports [S2].
cards.image_credit: Ullr · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Nanna
cards.flavor: The wife of Baldr; when Baldr died, Nanna followed him into grief (in some accounts she dies of sorrow).
cards.long: Nanna is the wife of Baldr. When Baldr died, Nanna was consumed by grief — in the Prose Edda she sets herself on Baldr's funeral pyre (in other accounts she dies of sorrow) [S2]. She is the mother of Fosite [S2].

cards.name: Forseti
cards.flavor: The son of Baldr, god of peace and reconciliation, who sits in the hall of Glitnir to settle disputes.
cards.long: Fosite (Forsétir) is the son of Baldr and Nanna, and a god of peace, reconciliation, and justice. He sits in the hall of Glitnir, where he settles all disputes, and his judgments are accepted by all [S2].
cards.image_credit: "Forseti zu Gericht sitzend" — Forseti sitting in judgement · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Magni
cards.flavor: The son of Thor (and the giantess Járnsaxa), a god of great strength.
cards.long: Magni is the son of Thor and the giantess Járnsaxa, a god of great strength. He and his brother Móði are the next generation of divine strength, destined to carry on after their father's death at Ragnarök [S2].

cards.name: Móði
cards.flavor: The son of Thor (and the giantess Járnsaxa), a god of great strength; brother of Magni.
cards.long: Móði is the son of Thor and the giantess Járnsaxa, brother of Magni. The two are the next generation of divine strength [S2].

cards.name: Járnsaxa
cards.flavor: The giantess who, with Thor, mothered Magni and Móði.
cards.long: Járnsaxa is a giantess who, in one account, is the mother of Thor's sons Magni and Móði [S2]. (Thor's mother is a separate, also-uncertain figure; Járnsaxa is the mother of his children with him, not his own mother.) [S2]
domains: the giantess mother of Thor's sons

cards.name: Gerðr
cards.flavor: The giantess whom Freyr loved and for whom he gave away his magic sword.
cards.long: Gerðr is a giantess whom Freyr saw and fell in love with. To win her, Freyr gave his magic sword (the one that fights by itself) to a dwarf as a gift, and as a result he is unarmed when Surt attacks at Ragnarök, and is slain [S2]. Gerðr is the cause of Freyr's fatal loss [S2].

cards.name: Skaði
cards.flavor: The huntress-goddess, associated with the mountains and skiing; she married Njord but the marriage failed.
cards.long: Skaði is a goddess of the hunt, the mountains, and skiing. She married Njord (the sea-god), but the marriage failed — she could not bear the sea, and he could not bear the mountains — and they separated [S2]. She is associated with winter and the mountains [S2].

cards.name: Surt
cards.flavor: The fire-giant of Muspelheim, who wields the great flame-sword and will destroy the world at Ragnarök.
cards.long: Surt is the fire-giant of Muspelheim, who wields a sword whose flame shines brighter than the sun [S1][S2]. At Ragnarök he marches against the gods, and he slays Freyr (who is unarmed, having given away his sword) [S1][S2]. Finally Surt hurls his flame over the whole world, destroying it [S1][S2].
cards.image_credit: Freyr and Surt do battle at Ragnarök · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

cards.name: Hrungnir
cards.flavor: The giant with the iron head and the iron belly, whom Thor slew with Mjölnir.
cards.long: Hrungnir is a giant whose head is of iron and whose belly is of iron, with razor-blades inside; he boasted that he would drain the mead-hall of the gods and kill them. Thor (disguised as a servant) accepted the challenge, and they drank; then Thor, revealed, struck Hrungnir with Mjölnir and killed him, and with a second blow crushed his iron head [S2].
domains: the giant of the iron head

cards.name: Svaðilfari
cards.flavor: The stallion of the unnamed hrímþurs who built the wall of Ásgarðr. Loki, transformed into a mare, lured Svaðilfari away from his work so the builder failed his deadline — and Loki bore Sleipnir as a mare.
cards.long: Gylfaginning IV–XIII: after the gods hired a giant builder to wall Ásgarðr, his horse Svaðilfari hauled stone at twice the speed of the gods' own carts, and the winter deadline loomed. The gods blamed Loki, who transformed himself into a mare; Svaðilfari ran after her, the builder lost the wager and was killed by Thor — and in that shape Loki bore the eight-legged foal Sleipnir ("in one account" the sources are explicit: Loki is Sleipnir's mother).
domains: the stallion of the frost-giant's builder

cards.name: Atum-Ra
cards.flavor: In the Heliopolitan tradition, the self-created god who rose from the primordial waters (Nun) as the first being; identified with Ra and with Atum (the 'Completed One').
cards.long: In the Heliopolitan (Heliopolis) creation tradition, the first god rose from the primordial waters of Nun — sometimes as a mound of earth (the benben), sometimes directly — and was named Atum, 'the Self-Completed.' He was identified with Ra, the sun god, and with Khepri, the scarab-headed morning sun [S1][S4]. From his own body (in one account, by spitting or sneezing) came Shu and Tefnut, the first divine pair [S1][S4]. The Heliopolitan account is only one of several Egyptian creation traditions; the Memphis tradition makes Ptah the self-created creator, and Hermopolis begins with a primeval Ogdoad of eight deities [S4]. We do NOT present one as 'the' Egyptian creation story — we present all three.
cards.image_credit: Ra Enthroned in the Tomb of Roy · — (Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Nun (the primordial waters)
cards.flavor: The primordial waters from which creation emerged — the infinite, dark water that existed before the world.
cards.long: Nun is the body of primordial waters that existed before creation. From Nun the first god rose (as Atum on the benben mound in Heliopolis) [S1][S4]. Nun is not exactly 'evil' — it is the undifferentiated pre-creation state — but it is also the state the world returns toward: the sun god must battle the serpent Apep (who represents the chaotic waters) every night in the Duat [S2][S4]. The priests of the temple performed the 'Opening of the Mouth' and other rites to keep the ordered world (Ma'at) separate from Nun [S4].

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Apep (Apophis)
cards.flavor: The great chaos serpent who tries each night to devour the sun god in the Duat; he is defeated every night — but must be defeated again.
cards.long: Apep (Apophis) is the great serpent of chaos who dwells in the primordial waters and tries every night to devour the sun god Ra as Ra travels through the Duat (the underworld) [S2][S4]. At the hour of the sun's weakest point (around midnight), Apep strikes; the sun god (helped by Thoth and others) defeats him — often with a knife or by the 'Eye of Ra' (Sekhmet) [S2][S4]. The defeat is repeated nightly: Apep is not permanently destroyed, he is merely driven back. This nightly battle is the mythic basis for the Egyptian understanding of the sun's daily rising [S2][S4]. Priests performed rites each night to 'bind' Apep [S4].
cards.image_credit: Ra slays Apep · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · CC BY-SA 3.0

sources.text: Book of the Dead (e.g., Papyrus of Ani)
Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Shu
cards.flavor: God of the air, son of Atum-Ra (with Tefnut); he holds up the sky (Nut) to keep it from the earth (Geb).
cards.long: Shu is the god of the air and the atmosphere, the first son of Atum-Ra [S1][S4]. He and his sister Tefnut (moisture) are the first divine pair born from the self-created god. Their children are Geb (earth) and Nut (sky) [S1][S4]. Shu's defining image is that of the supporter: he stands between earth and sky, holding Nut up with his hands so that the sky does not collapse onto the earth [S4]. He is a god of the ordered atmosphere — the space between the solid earth and the solid sky that the air (Shu) maintains [S4].
cards.image_credit: Shu · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · CC BY-SA 4.0

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Tefnut
cards.flavor: Goddess of moisture and rain, sister and consort of Shu; together they are the first divine pair.
cards.long: Tefnut is the goddess of moisture, rain, and the cool air, the sister and consort of Shu [S4]. She is the first divine pair with Shu, and their children are Geb and Nut [S1][S4]. Tefnut is also associated with the 'Eye of Ra' — in one myth she is the angry eye that Ra sent out to punish humanity, and who became Sekhmet (or was calmed and became Hathor) [S3][S4].
cards.image_credit: Tefnut · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · CC BY-SA 4.0

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Geb
cards.flavor: God of the earth, son of Shu and Tefnut; he is the father of Osiris, Isis, Set, and Nephthys.
cards.long: Geb is the god of the earth, the solid ground, the source of fertility [S4]. He is the son of Shu and Tefnut and the husband of Nut (his sister) [S1][S4]. Geb and Nut are the parents of the four children who form the core of the Osiris cycle: Osiris, Isis, Set, and Nephthys [S1][S4]. The myth of Geb and Nut: Shu separated them, holding Nut up, because the earth-god and the sky-goddess were inseparable [S4]. Geb's domain is the fertile black soil of the Nile, the source of all life [S4].

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Nut
cards.flavor: Goddess of the sky, daughter of Shu and Tefnut; she swallows the sun each night and gives it birth each morning.
cards.long: Nut is the goddess of the sky, the dome of the heavens studded with stars [S4]. She is the daughter of Shu and Tefnut and the wife of Geb (her brother) [S1][S4]. Nut's body arches over the earth: each night she swallows the sun (Ra) as it sets, carries it through her body through the night, and gives it birth again at dawn [S2][S4]. The sun's nightly journey through Nut's body is the same journey through the Duat (the underworld) where Apep waits [S2]. Nut is a goddess of the stars and of the cycle of death and rebirth that the sun performs daily [S4].
cards.image_credit: Nut (sky) crouching over Geb (earth) · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

sources.text: Book of the Dead (e.g., Papyrus of Ani)
Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Osiris
cards.flavor: The lord of the dead and resurrection; murdered by his brother Set, restored by Isis, and father of Horus; he judges the dead in the afterlife.
cards.long: Osiris is the lord of the dead, the god of resurrection, and the judge of the afterlife [S1][S2][S3][S4]. In the great myth, he was a just king of Egypt who was murdered by his jealous brother Set: Set placed him in a chest, sealed it with lead, and cast it into the Nile; the chest washed up in Byblos, and a tamarisk tree grew around it [S3][S4]. Isis found the body, restored it, and through their union conceived Horus [S3][S4]. Osiris then became lord of the Duat (the underworld), where he judges the dead: the 'Weighing of the Heart' (the heart weighed against the feather of Ma'at) determines the fate of the soul [S2][S4]. Osiris is the prototype of mummification: his restored body is the model for the mummified dead who seek resurrection [S4]. He is also associated with the annual Nile flood, which made the land fertile [S4].
cards.image_credit: Funerary stele of Tjrerei for Ra-Horakhty: Osiris, Horus, and Isis · State Museum of Egyptian Art, Munich (via Wikimedia Commons) · CC BY-SA 4.0

sources.text: Book of the Dead (e.g., Papyrus of Ani)
Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Isis
cards.flavor: The greatest of the Egyptian goddesses: wife of Osiris, mother of Horus, the master of magic, the protector of the dead, and the faithful wife.
cards.long: Isis is the most widely worshipped of the Egyptian goddesses and one of the most important figures in the Osiris cycle [S3][S4]. She is the sister and wife of Osiris and the mother of Horus [S1][S3][S4]. After Set murdered Osiris, Isis gathered the scattered pieces of his body (all except the genitals, which were lost) and used her magic to restore him and conceive Horus [S3][S4]. She is the master of magic (she is the one who, in one myth, learned the secret name of Ra and thereby gained his power) [S3][S4]. Isis is the protector of the dead: in the Book of the Dead, she appears as one of the four daughters of Horus who protect the canopic jars (the internal organs) [S2][S4]. Her worship spread across the Mediterranean and into the Roman world, where the 'Isis cult' persisted for centuries [S3][S4].
cards.image_credit: Isis (from a painted shroud) · Metropolitan Museum of Art (via Wikimedia Commons) · CC BY-SA 2.5

cards.name: Horus
cards.flavor: The falcon god of the sky and of kingship; son of Osiris and Isis; he avenges his father by defeating Set. The living pharaoh is Horus; the dead pharaoh becomes Osiris.
cards.long: Horus is the falcon god of the sky and of kingship [S4]. In the Osiris cycle, he is the son of Osiris and Isis, born after Osiris's murder, and his life's task is to avenge his father by defeating Set and reclaiming the throne [S3][S4]. The great myth of Horus vs. Set is a long, episodic struggle (preserved in the 'Contendings of Horus and Set') in which the two cousins fight for the throne of Egypt, judged by the Ennead [S4]. Horus wins, and becomes the king of the unified Egypt [S4]. The living pharaoh is identified with Horus (Horus 'so-and-so' is the pharaoh's name); the dead pharaoh becomes Osiris [S4]. There is also an 'elder' Horus (Harsomatus / the son of the first Horus) in some genealogies [S4]. The 'Eye of Horus' (the wedjat) is the broken-and-restored eye that Horus lost to Set and regained — a symbol of healing and protection [S4].
symbols: the wedjat eye (the Eye of Horus)
cards.image_credit: The Falcon God Horus · Walters Art Museum (via Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain
