cards.name: Set (Seth)
cards.flavor: The god of the desert, storm, and chaos; brother of Osiris who murdered him; the great enemy of Horus and of Ma'at (order).
cards.long: Set (Seth) is the god of the desert, the storm, chaos, and violence — the great antagonist of the Osiris cycle [S4]. He is the brother of Osiris and the one who murdered him, out of jealousy (Osiris was the rightful king) [S3][S4]. Set's defining act is the murder of Osiris: he lured Osiris to a banquet, measured him for a coffin, seized him, wrapped him in the coffin, sealed it with lead, and threw it in the Nile [S3][S4]. Set is then the great enemy of Horus (his nephew), and the two fight for the throne in the 'Contendings' [S4]. Set is the god of the foreign, the chaotic, the violent — the desert that threatens the fertile Nile valley [S4]. He is not simply 'evil': he is the necessary counterforce to Ma'at (order), the storm that keeps the world from stagnation [S4]. He was eventually 'demonized' as Egypt's enemies (the Libyans, then the Nubians, then the Persians) were associated with him [S4].
symbols: the Set animal (a mysterious creature with a long snout)
cards.image_credit: Horus and Seth crowning Ramesses III (detail of Seth) · — (Wikimedia Commons) · CC0

cards.name: Nephthys
cards.flavor: The goddess of the dead and the protection of the mummy; sister of Osiris and Isis; she helped Isis restore her brother.
cards.long: Nephthys is the goddess of the dead, the protection of the mummy, and the threshold (her name means 'lady of the house') [S4]. She is the sister of Osiris and Isis and the wife (in some accounts) of Set [S4]. In the Osiris cycle, Nephthys stands with Isis in grief and in the restoration of Osiris: the two sisters (Isis as the kite, Nephthys as the swallow) circle the body of Osiris, mourning and protecting it [S3][S4]. Nephthys is one of the four protectors of the canopic jars (the internal organs) in the Book of the Dead [S2][S4]. She is a goddess of the threshold — the boundary between the living and the dead — and of the protection of the mummy in the tomb [S4].
domains: the threshold (her name means 'lady of the house)

cards.name: Ra
cards.flavor: The sun god, king of the gods, who travels across the sky by day and through the Duat by night; he is defeated nightly by Apep and reborn each dawn.
cards.long: Ra is the sun god, the king of the gods, the creator (in the Heliopolitan tradition, as Atum-Ra) [S1][S4]. By day he crosses the sky in his solar barque (the 'Day Barque'), bringing light and life [S2][S4]. At sunset he enters the Duat (the underworld) in the 'Night Barque' and travels through the twelve hours of the night, where he faces Apep (the chaos serpent) at the hour of greatest danger (around midnight) [S2][S4]. Thoth and other gods help him defeat Apep, and he rises again at dawn [S2][S4]. Ra's nightly journey is the mythic basis of the Egyptian afterlife: the dead who are justified 'sail with Ra' through the night [S2][S4]. In the later (New Kingdom and after) period, Ra was fused with Amun to become 'Amun-Ra', the supreme god of the state religion [S4].

cards.name: Amun
cards.flavor: The 'Hidden One', the supreme god of the later Egyptian state religion; fused with Ra to become Amun-Ra.
cards.long: Amun is the 'Hidden One', a god who was originally a local god of Thebes but rose to become the supreme god of the Egyptian state religion in the New Kingdom and later periods [S4]. His name means 'the hidden one' — he is the invisible, the unseen, the source that is behind all things [S4]. Amun was fused with Ra to become 'Amun-Ra', the supreme creator and king of the gods [S4]. The great temple of Amun at Karnak was the largest temple complex in Egypt [S4]. Amun's 'hiddenness' made him a good candidate for fusion with other gods (Amun-Ra, Amun-Montu, etc.) [S4].
cards.image_credit: Statuette of Amun-Ra · State Museum of Egyptian Art, Munich (via Wikimedia Commons) · CC BY-SA 4.0

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Ptah
cards.flavor: The creator-god of Memphis, the divine craftsman who 'fashioned' the world in his heart and mouth; in the Memphite tradition he is the self-created first god.
cards.long: Ptah is the creator-god of Memphis, the patron of craftsmen and sculptors [S4]. In the Memphite creation tradition (preserved in the 'Memphite Theology' inscribed on a statue of Ptah-Sokar-Osiris), Ptah is the self-created first god who created the world 'in his heart and with his mouth' — that is, by thought (the heart) and by speech (the mouth), naming things into existence [S4]. This is a distinct creation tradition from the Heliopolitan (Atum-Ra) and the Hermopolitan (Ogdoad) accounts [S4]. Ptah is the divine craftsman: he is the patron of sculptors, metalworkers, and all makers, and the temple workshops at Memphis were centers of artistic production [S4]. Ptah was later fused with Sokar (aMemphite god of the necropolis) and with Osiris to become 'Ptah-Sokar-Osiris' [S4].
symbols: the ankh, was-sceptre, and djed (his triple symbol)
cards.image_credit: Statue of Ptah · The Metropolitan Museum of Art · CC0

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Thoth
cards.flavor: The ibis-headed god of wisdom, writing, and the moon; he records the verdict in the Weighing of the Heart and helps Ra defeat Apep.
cards.long: Thoth is the ibis-headed god of wisdom, writing, and the moon [S4]. He is the scribe of the gods: he records the verdict in the 'Weighing of the Heart' (the judgment of the dead) [S2][S4]. He is the inventor of writing (hieroglyphs) and of magic [S4]. In the solar journey, Thoth helps Ra defeat Apep at the critical midnight hour [S2][S4]. Thoth is also associated with the moon (his name is linked to the 'calculations' of the lunar calendar) [S4]. He is a god of order and knowledge — the opposite of the chaos that Apep represents [S4].
cards.image_credit: Thoth-Ibis · Walters Art Museum (via Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain

cards.name: Hathor
cards.flavor: The cow goddess of love, music, dance, and joy; she is the 'Great One' and the mother of the pharaoh; in the 'Eye of Ra' myth she becomes Sekhmet.
cards.long: Hathor is the cow goddess of love, music, dance, and joy, the 'Great One' and the mother of the pharaoh [S4]. She is the goddess of the western desert (the land of the dead) and of the mining regions (the turquoise mines of Serabit el-Khadim) [S4]. In the 'Eye of Ra' myth, Hathor (or Tefnut) is the eye that Ra sends out to punish humanity for plotting against him; the eye becomes enraged and is transformed into Sekhmet (the warrior goddess), and is calmed (by a trick involving red-dyed water that looks like blood) and returns as Hathor [S3][S4]. Hathor is the patroness of music and dance: her priests played the sistrum and the menat [S4]. She is also the 'mistress of the West' — the goddess who receives the dead [S4].
symbols: the cow's horns and solar disc
cards.image_credit: Head in Relief of the Egyptian Celestial Goddess Hathor · — (Wikimedia Commons) · CC BY-SA 2.0

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Bastet
cards.flavor: The cat goddess of the home, the protection of women, and the gentle aspects of the moon; the 'gentle' counterpart of Sekhmet.
cards.long: Bastet is the cat goddess of the home, the protection of women, and the gentle aspects of the moon [S4]. She is the 'gentle' counterpart of Sekhmet (the warrior goddess): where Sekhmet is the raging eye of Ra, Bastet is the calm, protective cat [S4]. Her great cult center was at Bubastis, where a great festival was held in her honor [S4]. Cats were sacred to Bastet: mummified cats were buried in great numbers at Bubastis and other sites [S4]. Bastet is a goddess of the domestic, the protective, the gentle — the opposite of the violent desert [S4].
cards.image_credit: Statuette of the goddess Bastet (bronze) · Museo Egizio, Turin (C 268, via Wikimedia Commons) · CC0

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Sekhmet
cards.flavor: The lioness goddess of war and destruction; the 'raging eye of Ra' who is calmed back into Hathor.
cards.long: Sekhmet is the lioness goddess of war, destruction, and the raging aspects of the sun [S4]. She is the 'eye of Ra' in her enraged form: when Ra sends his eye out to punish humanity, it becomes Sekhmet, who slaughters the rebels [S3][S4]. To calm her, Ra (or Thoth) devises a trick: he brews a potion dyed red with beet juice (to look like blood) and floods the land with it; Sekhmet, thinking she has drunk the blood of her victims, becomes drunk and calm, and returns as Hathor [S3][S4]. Sekhmet is the warrior goddess, the patron of the pharaoh in battle, and the destructive power of the sun [S4].
cards.image_credit: Granite Statue of Sitting Lioness Goddess Sekhmet · — (Wikimedia Commons) · Public domain

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Anubis
cards.flavor: The jackal-headed god of mummification and the dead; he oversees the embalming of the body and guides the soul to the afterlife.
cards.long: Anubis is the jackal-headed god of mummification and the dead [S4]. He is the overseer of the embalming: in the 'Weighing of the Heart' scene, Anubis (or a priest in his guise) performs the weighing [S2][S4]. He is the god of the threshold of the tomb — the boundary between the world of the living and the world of the dead [S4]. Anubis is the 'foremost of the westerners' (the west is the land of the dead, where the sun sets) [S4]. In the Osiris cycle, Anubis is the one who mummifies Osiris's body, making him the first mummy [S3][S4]. He is a god of protection of the grave and of the safe passage of the soul to the afterlife [S4].
cards.image_credit: Anubis (Egyptian god) · — (Wikimedia Commons) · CC BY-SA 4.0

sources.text: Book of the Dead (e.g., Papyrus of Ani)
Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Nun & Naunet (primeval waters)
cards.flavor: In the Hermopolitan creation tradition, the primeval waters (Nun and his female counterpart Naunet) are the first of the Ogdoad — the eight primeval deities.
cards.long: In the Hermopolitan (Hermopolis) creation tradition, the world begins with the Ogdoad — a group of eight primeval deities representing the conditions of the primordial state [S4]. The first pair is Nun and Naunet, the primeval waters [S4]. The Ogdoad is a distinct creation account from the Heliopolitan (Atum-Ra) and Memphite (Ptah) traditions [S4].

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Heh & Hehet (primordial infinity)
cards.flavor: In the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, Heh and Hehet represent primordial infinity (the endless, the without-beginning).
cards.long: Heh and Hehet are the second pair of the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, representing primordial infinity — the endless, the without-beginning [S4]. They are the 'eternity' that underlies the other primeval conditions [S4].

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Kek & Kauket (primordial darkness)
cards.flavor: In the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, Khenunu and Khenunit represent primordial mystery (the hidden, the secret).
cards.long: Khenunu and Khenunit are the third pair of the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, representing primordial mystery — the hidden, the secret, the unknown [S4]. (Not to be confused with Khnum, the ram-headed creator-god of the Nile cataracts, who is a separate, later deity [S4].)

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Amun & Amaunet (primordial hiddenness)
cards.flavor: In the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, Sat and Satet represent primordial duration (the enduring, the lasting).
cards.long: Sat and Satet are the fourth pair of the Hermopolitan Ogdoad, representing primordial duration — the enduring, the lasting, the stable [S4].

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Horus the Elder (Harsomatus)
cards.flavor: In some genealogies, an 'elder' Horus (Harsomatus) is the father of the younger Horus (son of Osiris).
cards.long: In some Egyptian genealogies (especially the later 'syncrisis' that tried to merge the different traditions), there is an 'elder' Horus (Harsomatus, 'Horus of the South') who is the son of the original sky-falcon Horus and the father of the younger Horus (the son of Osiris and Isis) [S4]. This is one of the genuine complications in Egyptian genealogy: the sources do not consistently distinguish the 'sky-falcon' Horus from the 'son of Osiris' Horus [S4].
cards.image_credit: Haroeris (Horus the Elder) · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · CC BY-SA 2.0

sources.text: Hornung, 'The Ancient Egyptian Books of the Dead' / 'Nile Religion' (academic)

cards.name: Nebo (the Sky-Father)
cards.flavor: In folk (and partly reconstructed) belief, 'the sky' personified as the supreme heavenly father — the highest deity, above the named gods. Whether Nebo was a formal pre-Christian god or a folk Christianization is debated.
cards.long: 'Nebo' (the sky) was personified in Slavic folk belief as the supreme heavenly father — the 'sky-father' above all the named gods [S4][S5][S6]. In the folk (post-Christian) world, Nebo is the highest, a kind of supreme creator who sends the rain and the thunder [S5]. Scholars differ on whether Nebo was a formal pre-Christian deity or a folk concept that absorbed the role of the supreme sky-god (Perun) after Christianization [S6]. The name 'Nebo' itself is common across Slavic languages [S4]. We treat Nebo as the reconstructed supreme sky-father, noting that its pre-Christian status is debated [S6].
cards.image_credit: The Seven Gods of Slavic Theo-Cosmology · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

sources.text: 19th-20th c. Slavic ethnographic collections (Volkov, Ivanov, etc.)

cards.name: Perun
cards.flavor: The supreme thunder-god of the pre-Christian Slavs, the sky-father, god of thunder, lightning, war, and the sacred oak. His great idol stood on a hill in Kiev, destroyed in 980 CE.
cards.long: Perun is the supreme thunder-god of the pre-Christian Slavs — the sky-father, the god of thunder, lightning, war, and the sacred oak [S1][S2][S4][S5]. He was the head of the Kiev pantheon: in the Primary Chronicle, the pagan ruler Vladimir of Kiev (980 CE) erected a great wooden idol of Perun on a hill (the 'Khorivets' hill) by the Dnieper, with a golden head and beard, and a row of other gods below [S1][S3]. The 'Tale of the Destruction of the Idols' (a later retelling) describes the idol being dragged into the river and destroyed in 980 [S3]. Perun's attributes: the hammer (the weapon that hurls thunder/lightning), the sacred oak (his tree), the sacred fire (he was 'the fire-god' in some accounts — the sacred flame that was not extinguished) [S4][S5][S6]. Perun is the great antagonist of Veles (the underworld god) in the reconstructed 'Perun-Veles' conflict [S6]. Perun's role is comparable to the Indo-European sky-father (Zeus, Thor, Dyaus Pitar) [S6].

cards.name: Veles
cards.flavor: The god of the underworld, cattle, magic, and the serpent; son of Svarog; the great antagonist of Perun. His domain is the realm of the dead (Nav/Cherd).
cards.long: Veles (Volos, Velas) is the god of the underworld, cattle, magic, and the serpent [S1][S2][S4][S5]. He is the son of Svarog (the sky-father/craftsman god) [S6]. Veles's domain is the realm of the dead (Nav/Cherd) — the underworld — and the earth [S6]. He is the god of cattle (the 'cattle-god'), of wealth, of magic, and of the serpent (his animal) [S4][S5][S6]. The snake is a sacred symbol of Veles: the 'Veles-day' (May 22, later the feast of St. Nicholas) was associated with the awakening of the snakes (the 'Veles' snakes') and was a day of special taboos [S5]. Veles is the great antagonist of Perun in the reconstructed 'Perun-Veles' conflict: the sky-thunder-god vs. the underworld-serpent-god [S6]. This is a genuine reconstructed duality, not a single attested myth — we present it as a scholarly reconstruction [S6].

cards.name: Svarog (Svarozhich)
cards.flavor: The god of fire, smithing, and crafts; father of Veles; in some accounts a sky/sun god. His name is the root of 'Svarozhich' (the 'Svarog-son').
cards.long: Svarog (Svarozhich) is the god of fire, smithing, and crafts [S1][S2][S4][S5]. He is the father of Veles [S6]. In some accounts, Svarog is a sky/sun god (the 'heavenly' father), while in others he is the 'earthly' craftsman-god who works in the forge [S4][S6]. His name is the root of 'Svarozhich' ('the Svarog-son') — a name applied to the smith, the craftsman, and (in one folk account) to the ruler himself (the 'Svarozhich' as a royal title) [S5]. Svarog's fire is the forge-fire: the sacred, creative fire that shapes metal [S4][S5]. He is a patron of the smiths and the craftsmen [S5]. The relationship between Svarog and Perun's 'sacred fire' is debated: some attribute the sacred fire to Svarog, others to Perun [S4][S6].

cards.name: Dazhbog
cards.flavor: The 'day-god' or 'light-god' (his name means 'giving day' or 'giving light'); a sun god, in the Kiev pantheon.
cards.long: Dazhbog (Dazh'bozh) is the 'day-god' or 'light-god' — his name is generally interpreted as 'giving day' or 'giving light' (from 'dazh' = day, 'bog' = god) [S1][S2][S4][S5]. He is a sun/light god in the Kiev pantheon [S1][S2]. His exact role is less well-attested than Perun or Veles: the sources name him but give little detail [S4]. He is sometimes identified with the sun, sometimes with the daylight in general [S4][S6]. A solar cult (the 'Dazhbog' sun-worship) is attested in folk survivals [S5].
domains: the giver of light (his name means 'day-god' or 'light-god')
cards.image_credit: Dazhbog (folk-art depiction) · Wikimedia Commons (institution in source file) · Public domain

sources.text: Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let / Latopis povest' vremen'nykh let)

cards.name: Khors
cards.flavor: A solar god (a 'sun' deity) in the Kiev pantheon; less well-attested than Dazhbog.
cards.long: Khors (Kors) is a solar god in the Kiev pantheon [S1][S2]. His exact relationship to Dazhbog (the 'day-god') is unclear: the two are both solar/light deities, and their distinction is not well-defined in the sources [S4]. Khors is named in the idol list but given little detail [S4]. Some scholars see Khors as a 'solar' god and Dazhbog as a 'daylight' god; others see them as overlapping [S6].
symbols: the chariot (the sun's chariot, in some accounts)

cards.name: Stribog
cards.flavor: The god of the wind, the air, the breath of the sky; in the Kiev pantheon. The 'Stribog' is the wind itself in folk belief.
cards.long: Stribog is the god of the wind, the air, the breath of the sky [S1][S2][S4][S5]. In the Primary Chronicle, Stribog is named as the 'father of the winds' (he 'sends the winds') [S1]. In folk belief, the 'Stribog' is the wind itself, and the wind is sometimes personified as a deity [S5]. Stribog's role is clear (the wind-god) but his mythic biography is not attested [S4].

cards.name: Mokosh
cards.flavor: The goddess of fertility, the earth, weaving, and the fate (the spinning of destiny); in the Kiev pantheon. Her name is the root of the common Slavic word for 'moisture/wetness'.
cards.long: Mokosh (Mocoš) is the goddess of fertility, the earth, weaving, and the fate (the spinning of destiny) [S1][S2][S4][S5]. Her name is generally interpreted as related to the common Slavic word for 'moisture/wetness' (the life-giving wetness of the earth) [S4]. Mokosh is the patroness of women's work (weaving, spinning) and of the fate — the 'spinning of destiny' (the threads of life) [S5]. In folk belief, the 'Mokosh' is associated with the earth-mother, the fertility of the land, and the fate of the household [S5]. She is named in the Kiev idol list [S1][S2]. Her relationship to the 'fate-spinning' (the Moirai/Norns equivalent) is a reconstructed parallel [S6].

cards.name: Lada
cards.flavor: The goddess of spring, fertility, beauty, and the household; in folk belief the 'Lada' is the beloved, the beautiful one. Her status as a formal pre-Christian goddess is debated.
cards.long: Lada is the goddess of spring, fertility, beauty, and the household [S4][S5]. In folk belief, the 'Lada' is the beloved, the beautiful one (the word 'lada' means 'beautiful, lovely, harmonious') [S5]. Lada is associated with the spring, the blossoming, the fertility of the land, and the harmony of the household [S4][S5]. Her status as a formal pre-Christian goddess (vs. a folk concept) is debated: the 'Lada' is more clearly a folk deity than a member of the formal Kiev pantheon [S6]. She is a 'spring/fertility' goddess, comparable to the Indo-European spring-maidens [S6].

cards.name: Morana (Marena)
cards.flavor: The goddess of death and winter; in folk tradition the 'drowning of Marzanna' (an effigy of the winter-goddess) is a spring-ritual that 'kills' winter and 'calls' spring. Her pre-Christian status is debated.
cards.long: Morana (Marena, Morena) is the goddess of death and winter [S4][S5]. In folk tradition, the 'drowning of Marzanna' (the 'Marzanna'/'Morana' doll) is a spring-ritual: an effigy of the winter-goddess is made, carried around, and drowned in a river to 'kill' winter and 'call' spring [S5]. This is a well-attested folk ritual (the 'proshchanie s zimoi' = 'farewell to winter') [S5]. Morana's status as a formal pre-Christian goddess is debated: the 'Marzanna'/'Morana' is more clearly a folk death/winter figure than a member of the formal Kiev pantheon [S6]. She is the great antagonist of Jarilo (the spring/youth god) in the reconstructed seasonal cycle [S6].

cards.name: Jarilo (Kupala)
cards.flavor: The god of spring, youth, and the sun; in folk tradition the 'Kupala' night (the midsummer solstice) is a fire-and-water festival. His relationship to the 'Kupala' ritual is well-attested in folk tradition.
cards.long: Jarilo (Yarilo) is the god of spring, youth, and the sun [S4][S5]. In folk tradition, the 'Kupala' night (the midsummer solstice, around June 23/24) is a fire-and-water festival: bonfires are lit, people leap over the fire, and the 'Kupala' flower (the fern-flower) is sought [S5]. The 'Kupala' ritual is well-attested in folk tradition across Slavic lands [S5]. Jarilo's relationship to the 'Kupala' festival is debated: some see Jarilo as the 'Kupala' god (the spring/youth/sun god), others see the 'Kupala' as a separate (possibly older) water/sun ritual [S6]. Jarilo is the great antagonist of Morana (the winter/death goddess) in the reconstructed seasonal cycle [S6].

cards.name: Zorya (the Morning Stars)
cards.flavor: The goddess (or pair of goddesses) of the dawn and the morning star (Venus); the 'Zorya' is the 'gate' of the sky, the threshold between the human world and the divine. In folk belief the 'Zorya' is the 'guardian of the threshold'.
cards.long: Zorya (Zarja) is the goddess (or pair of goddesses) of the dawn and the morning star (Venus) [S4][S5]. The 'Zorya' is the 'gate' of the sky, the threshold between the human world and the divine [S5]. In folk belief, the 'Zorya' is the 'guardian of the threshold' — she opens and closes the 'gate of the sky' (the dawn) [S5]. There are two 'Zorya': the 'Zorya Voshodnyaya' (the Rising Star, the dawn) and the 'Zorya Zakatnaya' (the Setting Star, the dusk) [S5]. The 'Zorya' is a well-attested folk figure (the dawn, the morning star), though her status as a formal pre-Christian goddess is debated [S6].

cards.name: Cherd (Chert)
cards.flavor: The god of the underworld, the realm of the dead (Nav/Cherd); in folk (post-Christian) belief the 'Chert' (the devil) is a Christianization of the underworld-god. His pre-Christian status is debated.
cards.long: 'Cherd' (Chert) is the reconstructed god of the underworld, the realm of the dead (Nav/Cherd) [S6]. In folk (post-Christian) belief, the 'Chert' (the devil) is often seen as a Christianization of the pre-Christian underworld-god [S6]. The 'Cherd'/'Chert' is the lord of the underworld, the realm of the dead [S6]. His pre-Christian status is debated: the 'Chert' is more clearly a folk/Christian figure than a formal pre-Christian deity [S6]. We present Cherd as the reconstructed underworld-god, noting that his pre-Christian identity is uncertain [S6].

cards.name: An (the heavens)
cards.flavor: The sky god, the supreme deity of the Sumerian pantheon; 'An' means 'sky/heaven'. In the Akkadian period he is called Anu. Father of Enlil and (in some accounts) Enki.
cards.long: 'An' (Sumerian; 'Anu' in Akkadian) is the sky god, the supreme deity of the Sumerian pantheon [S5][S6]. 'An' means 'sky' or 'heaven' — the god is the sky itself, the highest of the three cosmic regions (heaven, earth, underworld) [S5]. In the Sumerian period, An was the head of the pantheon; in the Akkadian and Babylonian periods, his supremacy was increasingly ceded to Enlil (and later Marduk) [S1][S6]. An's symbol is the star (the five-pointed star) and his animal is the bull [S5][S6]. An's consort is Antu (Sumerian; 'Anatum' in some accounts) [S5]. An is the father of Enlil (the air/storm god) and, in some accounts, Enki (the freshwater god) [S5]. The 'An' is also a title: the 'An' is the divine, the 'godhead' itself [S5].
symbols: the horned crown (the crown of kingship)

cards.name: Ki (the earth)
cards.flavor: The earth goddess, the consort of An (the sky); the 'mother' of the world. In Sumerian cosmology, An (heaven) and Ki (earth) are the first pair.
cards.long: 'Ki' is the earth goddess, the consort of An (the sky) [S5]. In Sumerian cosmology, An (heaven) and Ki (earth) are the first pair — the 'parents' of the world [S5]. Ki is the 'mother' of the world, the ground, the earth [S5]. The name 'Ki' is also the root of 'Kish' (a city) and of the 'ki' in 'kigurra' (a ritual object) [S5]. Ki is less well-attested as a deity than An: she is the earth-principle, the 'mother' of the world [S5].

cards.name: Apsu (the primeval freshwater)
cards.flavor: The primeval freshwater, the 'deep' beneath the earth; in the Atrahasis and Enuma Elish, Apsu is the god of the fresh water who is slain (in Atrahasis) or overthrown (in Enuma Elish).
cards.long: 'Apsu' (also 'Abzu') is the primeval freshwater, the 'deep' beneath the earth — the sweet water that underlies the world [S3][S5]. In Sumerian cosmology, Apsu (the fresh water) and Tiamat (the salt water) are the two primeval waters [S3][S5]. In the Atrahasis, Apsu (the god of the fresh water) is slain by Enki (and the gods) because his noise (the noise of humanity) disturbs his rest [S3]. In the Enuma Elish, Apsu's role is taken by Apsu (the fresh water) who is slain by Ea (Enki's Akkadian name) [S1]. Apsu is the 'deep', the primeval fresh water, the source of life [S3][S5].
domains: the sweet water beneath the earth

cards.name: Tiamat
cards.flavor: The primeval saltwater, the 'salt sea', the embodiment of chaos; in the Enuma Elish she is the great adversary of Marduk, whose slain body is used to create the world.
cards.long: 'Tiamat' is the primeval saltwater, the 'salt sea', the embodiment of the primordial state [S1][S5]. In Sumerian cosmology, Tiamat (the salt water) and Apsu (the fresh water) are the two primeval waters [S3][S5]. In the Enuma Elish, Tiamat is the great adversary of Marduk: she raises an army of monsters (led by Kingu) to fight Marduk, and is slain by Marduk, who splits her body in two to make the sky (the upper half) and the earth (the lower half) [S1]. Tiamat is the embodiment of chaos, the 'salt sea', the primordial state from which the ordered world emerges [S1][S5].

cards.name: Kingu
cards.flavor: The general of Tiamat's army in the Enuma Elish; he holds the 'Tablet of Destinies' (the symbol of cosmic authority); he is slain by Marduk.
cards.long: Kingu is the general of Tiamat's army in the Enuma Elish [S1]. He holds the 'Tablet of Destinies' (the 'me' of kingship, the symbol of cosmic authority) on Tiamat's behalf [S1]. Marduk slays Kingu and takes the Tablet of Destinies; from Kingu's blood, Marduk creates humanity (in the Enuma Elish) [S1]. Kingu is the 'crown' (his title: he holds the 'Tablet of Destinies') [S1].
domains: the 'crown' (his title: he holds the 'Tablet of Destinies')

cards.name: Enlil
cards.flavor: The 'air/wind/storm' god, the 'breath' of the world; in the Akkadian and Babylonian periods he is the king of the gods. His great temple was at Nippur. He is the 'decider' — he makes the fates (the 'me').
cards.long: 'Enlil' (Akkadian 'Ellil') is the 'air/wind/storm' god, the 'breath' of the world — his name means 'the breath of Enlil' (the wind that gives life) [S5][S6]. In the Sumerian period, Enlil was one of the great gods; in the Akkadian and Babylonian periods, he became the king of the gods (the 'Anum' — the supreme deity) [S1][S6]. Enlil's great temple was at Nippur (the 'Ekur' — the 'mountain house') [S5][S6]. Enlil is the 'decider': he makes the fates (the 'me' — the divine decrees that order the world) [S5]. Enlil's consort is Ninlil [S5]. Enlil's children include Nanna (the moon god), Ninhursag (the earth-mother, in some accounts), and Nergal (the underworld god, in some accounts) [S5]. Enlil is the god who decrees the flood (in the Atrahasis and the Gilgamesh flood-story) [S2][S3].
sacred_objects: the horned crown (the symbol of kingship)
cards.image_credit: Seated statue of Enlil · Iraq Museum, Baghdad · CC BY-SA 4.0

cards.name: Enki (Ea)
cards.flavor: The freshwater god of wisdom, magic, and the 'me' (the divine decrees); his great temple was at Eridu (the oldest city in Sumerian tradition). In the Atrahasis and the Gilgamesh flood-story, he saves the flood-hero against Enlil's will.
cards.long: 'Enki' (Sumerian; 'Ea' in Akkadian) is the freshwater god of wisdom, magic, and the 'me' (the divine decrees) [S5][S6]. His great temple was at Eridu (the 'Aabzu' — the 'house of the deep'), the oldest city in Sumerian tradition [S5][S6]. Enki is the god of wisdom, magic, and the 'me' — the divine decrees that order the world [S5]. He is the 'apku' (the sage), the patron of the scribes and the craftsmen [S5]. In the Atrahasis and the Gilgamesh flood-story, Enki (Ea) saves the flood-hero (Atrahasis/Utnapishtim) against Enlil's will, by whispering to the hero to build a boat [S2][S3]. Enki is the father of Nabu (the god of writing) [S5]. Enki's 'slanding' of Apsu (in the Atrahasis) is the creation-of-humanity story [S3].
symbols: the goat-fish (the 'adapa' fish, in some accounts)

cards.name: Ninlil
cards.flavor: The consort of Enlil; in some accounts she is the moon-goddess (or the 'light' of Enlil). She is the mother of Nanna (the moon god).
cards.long: Ninlil is the consort of Enlil [S5]. In some accounts, she is the moon-goddess (or the 'light' of Enlil) [S5]. She is the mother of Nanna (the moon god) [S5]. Ninlil's myth: in one Sumerian text, Enlil seduces Ninlil (while she is in the underworld), and she bears Nanna (the moon) there [S5]. Ninlil is the 'light' of Enlil — the moonlight that follows the storm-god [S5].

cards.name: Nanna (Sin)
cards.flavor: The moon god, the god of time, the calendar, and fate; his great temple was at Ur. In Sumerian tradition he is the son of Enlil; in Akkadian he is called Sin. Father of Utu (Shamash) and Inanna (Ishtar).
cards.long: 'Nanna' (Sumerian; 'Sin' in Akkadian) is the moon god, the god of time, the calendar, and fate [S5][S6]. His great temple was at Ur (the 'Ehursag') [S5][S6]. In Sumerian tradition, Nanna is the son of Enlil (and Ninlil) [S5]. In Akkadian, he is called Sin [S5]. Nanna is the father of Utu (the sun god, Akkadian 'Shamash') and Inanna (the love/war goddess, Akkadian 'Ishtar') [S5]. The moon-god decrees fates (the 'me') — the moon's phases are the measure of time [S5]. Nanna's 'time' role makes him the god of the calendar and of the measurement of the months [S5].

cards.name: Utu (Shamash)
cards.flavor: The sun god, the god of justice and the 'light' that reveals the truth; in Akkadian he is called Shamash. The sun-god travels through the underworld by night (the 'journey of the sun through the Duat' equivalent).
cards.long: 'Utu' (Sumerian; 'Shamash' in Akkadian) is the sun god, the god of justice and the 'light' that reveals the truth [S5][S6]. The sun-god travels across the sky by day and through the underworld by night (the 'journey of the sun') [S5]. Utu is the god of justice: he 'sees' all, and his light reveals the truth [S5]. In the 'Utnapishtim' flood-story and other texts, Utu is a 'judge' who sees the wickedness of humanity [S2]. Utu is the brother of Inanna (Ishtar) [S5]. Utu's 'justice' role makes him the patron of the oaths and the courts [S5].
symbols: the 'saw' (the sun's disc as a saw that cuts through the night)

cards.name: Inanna (Ishtar)
cards.flavor: The great goddess of love, sexuality, war, and fertility; 'queen of heaven'; the morning/evening star (Venus); her great temple was at Uruk. In Akkadian she is Ishtar. She descends to the underworld and is restored (the 'Inanna's Descent' myth).
cards.long: 'Inanna' (Sumerian; 'Ishtar' in Akkadian) is the great goddess of love, sexuality, war, and fertility [S4][S5][S6]. She is the 'queen of heaven', the morning/evening star (Venus) [S5]. Her great temple was at Uruk (the 'Eanna') [S5][S6]. Inanna is the most complex of the Mesopotamian deities: she is both the goddess of love and the goddess of war, both the life-giver and the death-bringer [S4][S5]. The great myth of 'Inanna's Descent to the Underworld': Inanna descends to the underworld to attend the funeral of her sister Ereshkigal (the underworld-goddess), is stripped of her powers at the seven gates, is killed, and is restored by Enki (who sends a being to bring her back) [S4][S5]. The 'Descent' is a myth of death and resurrection, and is one of the oldest attested 'descent-and-return' myths [S4][S5]. Inanna's 'Venus' role (the morning/evening star) makes her the goddess of the 'star' (the eight-pointed star is her symbol) [S5].

cards.name: Ereshkigal
cards.flavor: The queen of the underworld, the 'dark' goddess of the dead; Inanna's sister (in some accounts) or adversary. In the 'Descent' myth, Inanna attends her funeral (or is her guest) and is killed there.
cards.long: 'Ereshkigal' is the queen of the underworld, the 'dark' goddess of the dead [S4][S5]. She is the lord of the 'irigal' (the underworld) [S5]. In the 'Inanna's Descent' myth, Inanna descends to the underworld to attend Ereshkigal's funeral (or is her guest), and is killed there [S4][S5]. Ereshkigal is Inanna's sister (in some accounts) or her adversary [S4][S5]. Ereshkigal's consort is Nergal (the underworld-god, in some accounts) [S5]. Ereshkigal is the 'dark' counterpart of Inanna (the 'light' goddess) [S4][S5].

cards.name: Nergal
cards.flavor: The underworld god, the 'lord of the netherworld', the god of the plague; in some accounts he is Ereshkigal's consort. In the 'Nergal and Ereshkigal' myth, he 'rapes' (or marries) Ereshkigal and becomes her consort.
cards.long: 'Nergal' is the underworld god, the 'lord of the netherworld', the god of the plague [S5]. In some accounts, he is Ereshkigal's consort [S5]. The 'Nergal and Ereshkigal' myth: Nergal 'rapes' (or marries) Ereshkigal, and becomes her consort and the lord of the underworld [S5]. Nergal is the god of the plague and the 'dark' power of the underworld [S5]. He is also a war-god (in some accounts) [S5]. Nergal's 'plague' role makes him a feared deity — his 'dark' power is the power of death and disease [S5].

cards.name: Marduk
cards.flavor: The Babylonian supreme god, the 'storm' god, the king of the gods in the Babylonian period; in the Enuma Elish he slays Tiamat and creates the world from her body. His great temple was at Babylon (the Esagila).
cards.long: 'Marduk' is the Babylonian supreme god, the 'storm' god, the king of the gods in the Babylonian period [S1][S6]. In the Enuma Elish, Marduk is chosen by the gods to fight Tiamat; he slays her with his bow, net, and 'rakasu' winds, and splits her body in two to make the sky (the upper half) and the earth (the lower half) [S1]. From Kingu's blood (Tiamat's general), Marduk creates humanity [S1]. Marduk takes the 'Tablet of Destinies' (the symbol of cosmic authority) from Kingu [S1]. Marduk's great temple was at Babylon (the Esagila) [S6]. Marduk's 'supremacy' is a political/theological development: as Babylon rose to power (Old Babylonian period, c. 2000-1600 BCE), Marduk rose to be the king of the gods [S1][S6]. The Enuma Elish (the 'New Year' festival text) is the great myth of Marduk's supremacy [S1].

cards.name: Antu (Anatum)
cards.flavor: The consort of An (the sky god); the 'sky' as a female principle (in some accounts).
cards.long: 'Antu' (also 'Anatum') is the consort of An (the sky god) [S5]. She is the 'sky' as a female principle (in some accounts) [S5]. Antu is less well-attested as a distinct deity than An; she is the 'consort of the sky' [S5].

cards.name: Ninhursag
cards.flavor: The 'earth-mother', the 'mistress of the mountains'; in some accounts a consort of Enlil or a mother-figure. Her name means 'Lady of the Mountain'.
cards.long: 'Ninhursag' (also 'Nin-hursag') is the 'earth-mother', the 'mistress of the mountains' — her name means 'Lady of the Mountain' [S5]. She is a mother-figure in the Sumerian pantheon, the 'mother' of the gods (in some accounts) [S5]. Ninhursag is the 'earth' as a female principle [S5]. She is less well-attested as a distinct deity than the great gods; she is the 'earth-mother' principle [S5].

cards.name: Ningal
cards.flavor: The consort of Nanna (the moon god); the 'light' of the moon.
cards.long: 'Ningal' is the consort of Nanna (the moon god) [S5]. She is the 'light' of the moon [S5]. Ningal is less well-attested as a distinct deity than Nanna; she is the 'consort of the moon' [S5].

cards.name: Nabu
cards.flavor: The god of writing and wisdom, the patron of the scribes; son of Enki (Ea).
cards.long: 'Nabu' is the god of writing and wisdom, the patron of the scribes [S5]. He is the son of Enki (Ea) [S5]. Nabu is the 'sage' (the 'apku') and the patron of the scribal arts [S5]. His great temple was at Nippur (the 'Ezida') [S5].
